1.diff:
diff --git a/.github/workflows/rust.yml b/.github/workflows/rust.yml
index 9fd45e0..9251988 100644
--- a/.github/workflows/rust.yml
+++ b/.github/workflows/rust.yml
@@ -1,4 +1,4 @@
-name: Rust
+name: CI
 
 on:
   push:
@@ -11,12 +11,112 @@ env:
 
 jobs:
   build:
+    name: Build & test (${{ matrix.os }})
+    strategy:
+      fail-fast: false
+      matrix:
+        os: [ubuntu-latest, windows-latest, macos-latest]
+    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}
+    steps:
+      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
+      - uses: dtolnay/rust-toolchain@stable
+        with:
+          components: clippy, rustfmt
+      - uses: Swatinem/rust-cache@v2
+
+      - name: Build
+        run: cargo build --verbose
+
+      # Unit tests only; live-smoke below is the integration gate.
+      - name: Test
+        run: cargo test --verbose
 
-    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
+      # Non-blocking until the existing warning/format baseline is cleaned up.
+      - name: Clippy (non-blocking)
+        continue-on-error: true
+        run: cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings
 
+      - name: Format check (non-blocking)
+        continue-on-error: true
+        run: cargo fmt --all --check
+
+  # Attach to a real interpreter and decode its GC stats, per (OS, Python minor).
+  # Covers both finding paths (symbol lookup ≤3.12, "xdebugpy" cookie 3.13+) across
+  # all three binary parsers. Rationale for the full cross-product, and the
+  # platform defects it found, are in docs/adr/0004-per-platform-image-layout.md.
+  live-smoke:
+    name: gc-stats smoke (${{ matrix.os }} py${{ matrix.python }})
+    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}
+    strategy:
+      fail-fast: false
+      matrix:
+        # 3.16 omitted: not in the setup-python registry yet.
+        os: [ubuntu-latest, windows-latest, macos-latest]
+        python: ['3.8', '3.9', '3.10', '3.11', '3.12', '3.13', '3.14', '3.15']
+        # macOS only: 3.13+ ships com.apple.security.get-task-allow (PEP 768) so it
+        # attaches unprivileged; 3.8-3.12 does not and needs root. Flagged per
+        # version here because GitHub expressions cannot compare versions.
+        include:
+          - { python: '3.8',  macos_needs_root: 'yes' }
+          - { python: '3.9',  macos_needs_root: 'yes' }
+          - { python: '3.10', macos_needs_root: 'yes' }
+          - { python: '3.11', macos_needs_root: 'yes' }
+          - { python: '3.12', macos_needs_root: 'yes' }
     steps:
-    - uses: actions/checkout@v4
-    - name: Build
-      run: cargo build --verbose
-    - name: Run tests
-      run: cargo test --verbose
+      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
+      - uses: dtolnay/rust-toolchain@stable
+      - uses: Swatinem/rust-cache@v2
+      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
+        with:
+          python-version: ${{ matrix.python }}
+          # Required for 3.15, which is beta-only; no effect on stable minors.
+          allow-prereleases: true
+
+      - name: Build gcscope
+        run: cargo build --verbose
+
+      - name: Allow ptrace (best-effort)
+        if: runner.os == 'Linux'
+        run: sudo sysctl -w kernel.yama.ptrace_scope=0 || true
+
+      # macOS gates attach behind task_for_pid. Non-blocking so a failure here
+      # cannot skip the steps below and hide their result.
+      - name: Configure macOS taskport permissions
+        if: runner.os == 'macOS'
+        continue-on-error: true
+        run: |
+          id $(whoami)
+          sudo security authorizationdb write system.privilege.taskport is-developer
+          sudo security authorizationdb read system.privilege.taskport
+
+      # Dumps image facts (fat slices, PyRuntime section, symbol spelling, code
+      # signature) so a macOS failure is diagnosable without another CI round-trip.
+      - name: Describe the macOS Python image
+        if: runner.os == 'macOS'
+        continue-on-error: true
+        run: |
+          PYBIN="$(python -c 'import sys; print(sys.executable)')"
+          # The executable is a stub; the runtime lives in the framework dylib.
+          FW="$(python -c 'import sysconfig,os; print(os.path.join(sysconfig.get_config_var("prefix"), "Python"))')"
+          for f in "$PYBIN" "$FW"; do
+            echo "===== $f ====="
+            [ -e "$f" ] || { echo "(absent)"; continue; }
+            file "$f"
+            otool -l "$f" 2>/dev/null | grep -B2 -A4 'PyRuntime' || echo "(no PyRuntime section)"
+            nm -m "$f" 2>/dev/null | grep -i 'pyruntime\|py_version' || echo "(no matching symbols)"
+            codesign -dv --entitlements - "$f" 2>&1 | grep -i 'flags\|runtime\|get-task-allow' \
+              || echo "(unsigned / no signing info)"
+          done
+
+      # Kept unprivileged where it works, so a target that stops shipping
+      # get-task-allow fails here instead of being masked by blanket sudo.
+      - name: Attach, detect version, assert non-empty GC stats
+        if: runner.os != 'macOS' || matrix.macos_needs_root != 'yes'
+        run: python tests/live_smoke.py --label ${{ matrix.os }}-py${{ matrix.python }}
+
+      - name: Attach, detect version, assert non-empty GC stats (sudo)
+        if: runner.os == 'macOS' && matrix.macos_needs_root == 'yes'
+        run: |
+          PY="$(command -v python)"
+          sudo -E "$PY" tests/live_smoke.py \
+            --label ${{ matrix.os }}-py${{ matrix.python }}
diff --git a/README.md b/README.md
index 97dd7ba..c9569fc 100644
--- a/README.md
+++ b/README.md
@@ -13,6 +13,34 @@ Cross-platform CLI tool for reading and analyzing CPython process memory.
 
 `-1` can be used as PID to target the current process.
 
+## Attaching: per-platform permissions
+
+gcscope reads another process's memory, which every OS gates differently.
+
+| Platform | Requirement |
+|---|---|
+| **Windows** | None for a process you own. |
+| **Linux** | Same-uid works when the target is a descendant. Otherwise loosen Yama: `sudo sysctl -w kernel.yama.ptrace_scope=0`. |
+| **macOS** | Depends on the target: **Python 3.13+ attaches unprivileged**; **3.8–3.12 needs `sudo gcscope …`**. |
+
+On macOS the split is the target's doing: framework builds are signed with a
+hardened runtime, and only 3.13+ ships `com.apple.security.get-task-allow` (with
+PEP 768), which is what admits a same-user caller. Granting
+`system.privilege.taskport` does not help. If you don't know the target's version,
+use `sudo`.
+
+To avoid `sudo` there, sign gcscope with `com.apple.security.cs.debugger` — the
+mechanism LLDB's `debugserver` uses:
+

+# 0004 — Per-platform image layout is discovered, not assumed
+
+**Status:** Accepted — implemented 2026-07-20.
+
+## Context
+
+Runtime finding ([ADR 0002](0002-version-split-runtime-finding.md)) reaches the
+target's binary through three format-specific paths — `find_section_in_{elf,pe,macho}`
+and `resolve_symbol_{elf,pe,macho}`. All development happened on Windows/PE; the
+other two formats compiled, were reachable, and had never executed against a real
+process. The first live smoke matrix across all three platforms failed every
+non-Windows leg — Linux 3.13+ (3/8) and macOS entirely (8/8) — on five defects,
+none version-related, each a place where PE-shaped facts were assumed universal:
+
+1. **ELF section names are dotted.** CPython's `GENERATE_DEBUG_SECTION`
+   (`Include/internal/pycore_debug_offsets.h`) emits `section("." #name)` on Linux
+   only, so the section is `.PyRuntime` on ELF, `PyRuntime` on Mach-O, and
+   `PyRuntim` on PE (8-char truncation). The ELF branch matched the undotted
+   spelling, so the 3.13+ cookie path had **never** worked on Linux.
+2. **macOS images are universal binaries.** The Python framework ships
+   `universal2`, so offset 0 holds a fat header and `MachO::parse(bytes, 0)` failed
+   outright — at all three Mach-O call sites.
+3. **Mach-O decorates C symbols.** `_PyRuntime` is stored as `__PyRuntime`,
+   `Py_Version` as `_Py_Version`.
+4. **A fat slice must be parsed as a standalone buffer.** Unwrapping in place
+   (`MachO::parse(bytes, slice_start)`) is not enough: a slice's internal *file*
+   offsets (`symtab.symoff`/`stroff`, `section.offset`) are slice-relative, and
+   goblin indexes them into whatever buffer it is given. It therefore read the
+   symbol table out of the wrong slice and returned **no symbols at all**. The
+   slice must be cut out and parsed at offset 0.
+5. **The macOS image base is not the lowest mapping.** The kernel attributes
+   low-address reservations to the image path, so the first mapping is a no-access
+   `---` range ~14 MB below the image. The Mach-O header sits at the start of
+   `__TEXT`, the executable mapping, and section `vmaddr`s are relative to that.
+   ELF/PE are the opposite: their first mapping *is* the load base.
+
+Defects 1–3 fail *closed* — the parse fails and the error is honest. The other two
+do not, which is why they survived:
+
+- **4 failed silently.** An empty symbol table is indistinguishable from a stripped
+  binary, and it broke only symbol-driven paths while leaving address-driven ones
+  (`vmaddr`, `n_value`) green. That split coincides exactly with the 3.13 version
+  boundary, so a single format bug presented as a version-specific one.
+- **5 failed open.** The wrong base still pointed into a mapped `rw-` region, so
+  reads succeeded and returned garbage. Only the `"xdebugpy"` cookie caught it.
+
+The lesson worth keeping: **a partially-correct fix for a format quirk is worse
+than none**, because it relocates the failure to something that looks like a
+different problem.
+
+## Decision
+
+**Per-platform image facts belong in `memory/binary.rs` and the format-specific
+finders, and each must be confirmed by a live CI leg rather than inferred from the
+format spec.**
+
+- Section lookup accepts every spelling a platform emits (`.PyRuntime` /
+  `PyRuntime` / `PyRuntim`).
+- All Mach-O parsing goes through **`binary::parse_macho`**, which selects the
+  host-architecture slice, cuts it out and parses it at offset 0, and returns the
+  image plus the slice's start offset. Callers using virtual addresses ignore the
+  offset; callers using *file* offsets (`sect.offset`) add it. Both halves matter:
+  parse standalone or the symbol table is silently empty; rebase file offsets or
+  reads land in the wrong slice.
+- Symbol matching accepts the undecorated name or an underscore-prefixed one.
+- `find_python_modules` picks the image base per platform — first executable
+  mapping on macOS, first mapping elsewhere — `cfg`-gated so ELF/PE are untouched.
+
+## Consequences
+
+- All 24 legs green (3 OSes × Python 3.8–3.15); `live-smoke` is a blocking gate.
+- ADR 0002's open question on ELF/Mach-O symbol visibility is **answered for both**.
+  The documented data-segment scan fallback remains unnecessary everywhere.
+- **macOS attach privilege is a property of the target.** Every framework build is
+  hardened (`flags=0x10000(runtime)`), but only 3.13+ carries
+  `com.apple.security.get-task-allow`, which lets a same-user caller take the task
+  port; 3.8–3.12 returns `EPERM` and needs root. Granting
+  `system.privilege.taskport` does not change this. The entitlement ships with PEP
+  768 remote-debugging support, so unprivileged attach to 3.13+ is a supported
+  configuration. CI encodes the split rather than running macOS under blanket root,
+  so a build that stops shipping the entitlement fails instead of being masked.
+- `find_runtime_pre_3_13` reports per module whether the symbol resolved and to what
+  address, rather than collapsing "symbol missing" and "offsets disagree" into one
+  message. That distinction is what located defect 4.
+- Two fixes are **correct-but-inferred** and should be revisited:
+  - `parse_macho` selects the slice by `cfg!(target_arch)` — *gcscope's*
+    architecture, not the target's. A universal2 Python under Rosetta read by an
+    arm64 gcscope would pick the wrong slice and compute a wrong address
+    **silently**. The correct key is the target process's architecture.
+  - "First executable mapping is the base" holds only because `__TEXT` is `r-x` and
+    carries the header. The rigorous source is dyld (`task_dyld_info` / image list).
+- Every one of the five was found by *running* the matrix; each attempt to reason
+  ahead of it picked the wrong culprit. The cheap diagnostics that settled them —
+  `file`/`otool`/`nm`/`codesign` on the image, a mapped-region dump on failure, and
+  the per-module symbol-vs-cross-reference breakdown — are retained in the workflow
+  and in `tests/live_smoke.py`.
+
+## Verification
+
+The live smoke matrix — 3 OSes × Python 3.8–3.15, one leg per pair; see
+`docs/tests-harness-plan.md`. A platform assumption that regresses fails the
+specific `(os, version)` leg that depends on it.

+/// Parse a Mach-O image, transparently unwrapping a universal ("fat") binary.
+///
+/// macOS ships Python as a framework built `universal2` (x86_64 + arm64), so
+/// offset 0 holds a *fat header* rather than a Mach-O header and a plain
+/// `MachO::parse(bytes, 0)` fails outright. Every macOS code path — both the
+/// `PyRuntime` section lookup and symbol resolution — has to go through here.
+///
+/// gcscope reads a process on the machine it runs on, so the slice to pick is
+/// the host architecture: the target executes that slice, and its addresses are
+/// the ones present in the process's memory map.
+///
+/// Returns the parsed image **and the slice's offset within `bytes`**. Callers
+/// working in virtual addresses (`vmaddr`, `n_value`) can ignore the offset;
+/// callers that index back into `bytes` with a *file* offset (`sect.offset`)
+/// must add it, because a slice's internal file offsets are relative to the
+/// start of that slice rather than the start of the fat file.
+pub fn parse_macho(bytes: &[u8]) -> Option<(goblin::mach::MachO<'_>, usize)> {
+    use goblin::mach::{Mach, MachO};
+
+    match Mach::parse(bytes).ok()? {
+        Mach::Binary(macho) => Some((macho, 0)),
+        Mach::Fat(fat) => {
+            let want = if cfg!(target_arch = "aarch64") {
+                goblin::mach::cputype::CPU_TYPE_ARM64
+            } else {
+                goblin::mach::cputype::CPU_TYPE_X86_64
+            };
+            for arch in fat.iter_arches().flatten() {
+                if arch.cputype != want {
+                    continue;
+                }
+                let start = arch.offset as usize;
+                let end = start.checked_add(arch.size as usize)?;
+                let slice = bytes.get(start..end)?;
+                // Parse the slice as a standalone image (offset 0), NOT in place
+                // via `MachO::parse(bytes, start)`. A slice's internal file
+                // offsets — `symtab.symoff`/`stroff`, `section.offset` — are
+                // relative to the slice, and goblin indexes them directly into
+                // whatever buffer it is handed. Parsing in place makes it read the
+                // symbol table from the wrong slice and silently yield **no
+                // symbols**, which is invisible to anything that only touches
+                // virtual addresses (`vmaddr`, `n_value`) and breaks everything
+                // that reads the symbol table.
+                return MachO::parse(slice, 0).ok().map(|m| (m, start));
+            }
+            None
+        }
+    }
+}

+"""Attach target: a process that keeps CPython's cyclic GC continuously busy.
+
+Usage:  python spin.py [max_seconds]
+
+Prints one flushed "READY <pid>" line once every generation has been collected at
+least once, so a harness can wait on that instead of sleeping a guessed interval.
+Self-terminates after max_seconds (default 120) so a crashed harness cannot orphan
+it.
+
+Must stay 3.8-compatible with no third-party imports: it runs unchanged against
+every interpreter in the test matrix.
+"""
+
+import gc
+import os
+import sys
+import time
+
+CYCLES_PER_BURST = 2000
+
+
+def make_garbage(count):
+    """Allocate `count` unreachable reference cycles and drop them.
+
+    Cycles are the point: a plain list would be reclaimed by refcounting and
+    never move the generation counters.
+    """
+    for _ in range(count):
+        a = {}
+        b = {"peer": a, "payload": [0] * 32}
+        a["peer"] = b
+        del a, b
+
+
+def main():
+    max_seconds = float(sys.argv[1]) if len(sys.argv) > 1 else 120.0
+
+    gc.enable()
+
+    # Seed every generation before READY, so a reader that attaches the instant it
+    # sees the marker isn't racing the first gen-2 collection.
+    make_garbage(CYCLES_PER_BURST)
+    for generation in range(3):
+        gc.collect(generation)
+
+    sys.stdout.write("READY %d\n" % os.getpid())
+    sys.stdout.flush()
+
+    # monotonic: a wall-clock jump must not shorten or extend the backstop.
+    deadline = time.monotonic() + max_seconds
+    tick = 0
+    while time.monotonic() < deadline:
+        make_garbage(CYCLES_PER_BURST)
+        # Rotate generations; a bare gc.collect() is full and only bumps gen 2.
+        gc.collect(tick % 3)
+        tick += 1
+        time.sleep(0.05)
+    return 0
+
+
+if __name__ == "__main__":
+    sys.exit(main())

+"""Live smoke driver: spawn a real interpreter, attach with gcscope, assert stats.
+
+Exercises the end-to-end pipeline (find `_PyRuntime` -> detect version -> read
+offsets -> decode GC generation stats) against a live process. Used by the
+`live-smoke` CI job and runnable by hand on any OS:
+
+    python tests/live_smoke.py                       # uses this interpreter
+    python tests/live_smoke.py --python C:/py38/python.exe --label py3.8
+
+Exit code 0 = PASS, 1 = FAIL (with the reason and the captured output).
+"""
+
+import argparse
+import os
+import subprocess
+import sys
+import time
+
+HERE = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))
+REPO = os.path.dirname(HERE)
+SPIN = os.path.join(HERE, "fixtures", "spin.py")
+
+SPIN_LIFETIME_SECS = 120
+READY_TIMEOUT_SECS = 20
+CMD_TIMEOUT_SECS = 60
+
+
+def default_gcscope():
+    exe = "gcscope.exe" if os.name == "nt" else "gcscope"
+    return os.path.join(REPO, "target", "debug", exe)
+
+
+def run(argv, timeout=CMD_TIMEOUT_SECS):
+    """Run a command, capturing merged output as text. Returns (rc, output)."""
+    try:
+        proc = subprocess.run(
+            argv,
+            stdout=subprocess.PIPE,
+            stderr=subprocess.STDOUT,
+            # Explicit: the default locale encoding chokes on gcscope's
+            # box-drawing output under a non-UTF-8 Windows code page.
+            encoding="utf-8",
+            errors="replace",
+            timeout=timeout,
+        )
+        return proc.returncode, proc.stdout or ""
+    except subprocess.TimeoutExpired:
+        # A hang is a real failure mode here (bad pointer walk on an unknown
+        # layout), so report it rather than letting CI stall.
+        return 124, "TIMEOUT after %ds: %s" % (timeout, " ".join(argv))
+
+
+def wait_for_ready(proc, log_path):
+    """Poll spin.py's log for READY; return the interpreter's PID, or None.
+
+    The PID comes from the marker rather than proc.pid so it stays correct if a
+    launcher or shim sits between us and the real interpreter.
+    """
+    deadline = time.monotonic() + READY_TIMEOUT_SECS
+    while time.monotonic() < deadline:
+        if proc.poll() is not None:
+            return None  # died on startup; caller prints the log
+        try:
+            with open(log_path, "r", encoding="utf-8", errors="replace") as fh:
+                for line in fh:
+                    if line.startswith("READY "):
+                        return int(line.split()[1])
+        except IOError:
+            pass  # not created yet
+        time.sleep(0.25)
+    return None
+
+
+def main():
+    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__)
+    parser.add_argument("--gcscope", default=default_gcscope(),
+                        help="path to the gcscope binary (default: target/debug)")
+    parser.add_argument("--python", default=sys.executable,
+                        help="interpreter to attach to (default: this one)")
+    parser.add_argument("--label", default=None,
+                        help="tag for PASS/FAIL lines (default: the target's version)")
+    parser.add_argument("--tmpdir", default=os.environ.get("RUNNER_TEMP") or
+                        os.path.join(REPO, ".temp"),
+                        help="scratch dir for the fixture log")
+    args = parser.parse_args()
+
+    if not os.path.exists(args.gcscope):
+        print("FAIL: gcscope binary not found at %s (run `cargo build` first)"
+              % args.gcscope)
+        return 1
+
+    rc, ver = run([args.python, "--version"])
+    if rc != 0:
+        print("FAIL: target interpreter is not runnable: %s" % ver.strip())
+        return 1
+    ver = ver.strip()
+    label = args.label or ver.replace("Python ", "py")
+    print("target: %s (%s)" % (ver, args.python))
+
+    def fail(reason, detail=""):
+        print("FAIL(%s): %s" % (label, reason))
+        if detail:
+            print(detail)
+        return 1
+
+    if not os.path.isdir(args.tmpdir):
+        os.makedirs(args.tmpdir)
+    log_path = os.path.join(args.tmpdir, "spin-%s.log" % label)
+
+    log = open(log_path, "w+", encoding="utf-8")
+    proc = subprocess.Popen(
+        [args.python, SPIN, str(SPIN_LIFETIME_SECS)],
+        stdout=log, stderr=subprocess.STDOUT,
+    )
+    try:
+        pid = wait_for_ready(proc, log_path)
+        if pid is None:
+            log.flush()
+            with open(log_path, "r", encoding="utf-8", errors="replace") as fh:
+                return fail("fixture never reported READY", fh.read())
+        print("spin.py ready as pid %d" % pid)
+
+        # Same attach path as gc-stats, so a failure here isolates *finding* from
+        # decoding.
+        print("----- find-runtime -----")
+        rc, out = run([args.gcscope, "find-runtime", str(pid)])
+        print(out)
+        if rc != 0:
+            # Separates "no python module was mapped" from "found it but the
+            # cookie/cross-reference check failed".
+            print("----- mapped python regions (diagnostic) -----")
+            _, regions = run([args.gcscope, "list", str(pid)])
+            shown = [ln for ln in regions.splitlines() if "ython" in ln]
+            print("\n".join(shown[:25]) if shown
+                  else "(no mapped region has a python path — "
+                       "module enumeration is the problem)")
+            return fail("could not locate _PyRuntime")
+
+        # Informational: read-runtime uses its own finder, not attach.
+        print("----- read-runtime (version, best-effort) -----")
+        _, out = run([args.gcscope, "read-runtime", str(pid)])
+        print("\n".join(out.splitlines()[:4]))
+
+        print("----- gc-stats -----")
+        rc, out = run([args.gcscope, "gc-stats", str(pid)])
+        print(out)
+        if rc != 0:
+            return fail("gc-stats exited %d" % rc)
+        if "No GC stats found." in out:
+            return fail("stats decoded empty")
+        if "Collections" not in out:
+            return fail("no stats table in output")
+
+        print("PASS(%s): attached + detected + decoded non-empty GC stats" % label)
+        return 0
+    finally:
+        if proc.poll() is None:
+            proc.kill()
+            proc.wait()
+        log.close()
+
+
+if __name__ == "__main__":
+    sys.exit(main())

+//! Timestamp conversion for trace exporters.
+//!
+//! CPython records GC timestamps in nanoseconds (`PyTime_t`); the Chrome trace
+//! format expects microseconds. This is the only arithmetic between a decoded
+//! `GcStat` and an emitted trace event.
+
+/// Convert a nanosecond timestamp to the microseconds a Chrome trace expects.
+///
+/// Integer division truncates toward zero, so sub-microsecond events collapse to
+/// the enclosing microsecond rather than rounding to the nearest one. That is
+/// deliberate: a GC pause shorter than 1 µs renders as a zero-width slice, which
+/// is honest, whereas rounding could push an `end` before its `begin`.
+pub fn ts_us(ts_ns: i64) -> i64 {
+    ts_ns / 1000
+}
+
+#[cfg(test)]
+mod tests {
+    use super::*;
+
+    #[test]
+    fn converts_nanoseconds_to_microseconds() {
+        assert_eq!(ts_us(0), 0);
+        assert_eq!(ts_us(1_000), 1);
+        assert_eq!(ts_us(1_000_000), 1_000);
+    }
+
+    /// Truncation toward zero, not rounding and not flooring — a begin/end pair
+    /// must never invert, which rounding at the boundary could cause.
+    #[test]
+    fn truncates_toward_zero() {
+        assert_eq!(ts_us(1_500), 1);
+        assert_eq!(ts_us(999), 0);
+        assert_eq!(ts_us(-1_500), -1);
+        assert_eq!(ts_us(-999), 0);
+    }
+
+    /// Monotonic-clock values are large; the conversion must not overflow at the
+    /// extremes of the type CPython hands us.
+    #[test]
+    fn handles_the_full_i64_range() {
+        assert_eq!(ts_us(i64::MAX), i64::MAX / 1000);
+        assert_eq!(ts_us(i64::MIN), i64::MIN / 1000);
+    }
+}

+    seen: &mut HashMap<(u32, usize), i64>,

+    let mut fresh: Vec<&GcStat> = Vec::new();
+    for stat in stats {
+        let mark = seen.entry((stat.generation, stat.slot)).or_insert(0);
+        if stat.ts_start > *mark {
+            *mark = stat.ts_start;
+            fresh.push(stat);
+        }
+    }

+
+    fn stat(generation: u32, slot: usize, ts_start: i64) -> GcStat {

+
+    fn fresh_ts(stats: &[GcStat], seen: &mut HashMap<(u32, usize), i64>) -> Vec<i64> {
+        select_fresh(stats, seen).into_iter().map(|s| s.ts_start).collect()

+    #[test]

+        assert!(fresh_ts(&stats, &mut seen).is_empty());

+        assert!(fresh_ts(&[stat(0, 0, 100)], &mut seen).is_empty());

+        assert_eq!(fresh_ts(&[stat(0, 0, 150)], &mut seen), vec![150]);

+    #[test]

+        let mut seen = HashMap::new();

+            stat(0, 1, 100),
+            stat(1, 0, 400),
+            stat(2, 0, 200),

+    }

+    fn marks_advance_only_for_the_slots_that_were_selected() {
+        let mut seen = HashMap::new();

+        assert_eq!(seen.get(&(1, 0)), Some(&0));

+#[cfg(test)]
+mod tests {

+
+    fn v(major: u8, minor: u8, micro: u8, release_level: u8, serial: u8) -> PythonVersion {
+        PythonVersion { major, minor, micro, release_level, serial }
+    }
+
+    #[test]
+    fn hex_round_trips_every_release_level() {
+        // One per level, including every hex the LAYOUTS registry can hold.
+        for hex in [
+            0x030800f0u64, // 3.8.0 final
+            0x030d01f0,    // 3.13.1 final
+            0x030f00a8,    // 3.15.0a8
+            0x030f00b1,    // 3.15.0b1
+            0x030f00c2,    // 3.15.0rc2
+            0x031000a0,    // 3.16.0a0
+        ] {
+            let parsed = PythonVersion::from_hex(hex).expect("valid hex");
+            assert_eq!(parsed.to_hex(), hex, "round-trip failed for {hex:#010x}");
+        }
+    }
+
+    #[test]
+    fn hex_decodes_each_field() {
+        let parsed = PythonVersion::from_hex(0x030f00b1).unwrap();
+        assert_eq!(parsed, v(3, 15, 0, 0xB, 1));
+    }
+
+    #[test]
+    fn hex_rejects_absent_major_and_minor() {
+        // The guard is on major AND minor both being zero — a zeroed read.
+        assert_eq!(PythonVersion::from_hex(0), None);
+        assert_eq!(PythonVersion::from_hex(0x0000_00f0), None);
+        // A zero major with a non-zero minor is still decoded (not our call to reject).
+        assert!(PythonVersion::from_hex(0x0001_0000).is_some());
+    }

+    }

+    fn from_string_rejects_non_versions() {
+        for s in ["", "3", "3.x", "x3.12", "..", "3."] {

+        }
+    }
+
+    #[test]
+    fn from_string_rejects_overflowing_component() {

+        // those guards "3.999.0" would wrap to a plausible-looking minor and gcscope
+        // would silently resolve the wrong layout.

+        for s in ["3.15.0a8", "3.15.0b1", "3.15.0rc1", "3.12.0", "3.8.19"] {

+  Observer's clock is the machine's monotonic counter, which is the one CPython times a
+  Collection with, so the two tiers are readings of the same thing and a mixed file aligns. The
+  distinction decision 5 draws is now about *which* reading a sample gets, not which clock:
+  a build with no timestamps takes the poll's, because it published none of its own.

+# 0021 — The Perfetto encoder is hand-rolled, and a decoder gcscope did not write is what makes that safe
+
+**Status:** Accepted — implemented 2026-08-09. First step of the Perfetto exporter, alongside
+[ADR 0008](0008-reader-consumer-package-layering.md)'s layering and the fan-out
+`monitor/exporters/combining.rs` already carries.
+
+## Context
+
+gcscope writes Chrome Trace JSON by hand: the shapes are small and fixed, the crate has no
+serde dependency, and a byte-for-byte gate pins the output. Perfetto's binary format is the
+second output an operator asked for, and it raises the same question with a different answer
+available. `prost` (or `protobuf-codegen`) would generate message types from Perfetto's
+`.proto` files and serialize them, and the numbers would be right by construction.
+
+The slice of the format gcscope needs is small — varints, length-delimited submessages, and
+about forty field numbers. gcmon writes the same traces from a 62-line encoder plus a
+hand-maintained table, and that table is directly transcribable.
+
+What makes the choice a real trade-off is how a hand-rolled encoder fails. gcmon shipped four
+bugs in this exact code: `TrackEvent.type` and `track_uuid` renumbered upstream, timestamps
+written inside `TrackEvent` where field 1 is a `timestamp_delta_us` oneof member,
+`DebugAnnotation.name` moving from field 1 to field 10, and a varint masked to 32 bits that
+wrote `sibling_order_rank = -1` as `0`. Every one of them produced a trace that **parsed**. It
+rendered wrong, and a human opening the UI is what caught it. That is the failure mode
+[ADR 0004](0004-per-platform-image-layout.md) names for image layout — it fails *open*, the
+read lands somewhere plausible and returns garbage — arriving in a second subsystem.
+
+Generating from the `.proto` would remove the field-number risk and add: a build dependency
+that compiles protobuf schemas, a vendored copy of Perfetto's `.proto` tree to keep current,
+and a generated-code layer between `TraceEvent` and the bytes. gcscope already owns one
+hand-maintained table of numbers-that-must-be-right — the CPython struct offsets — and the
+whole of `remote_debugging/offsets/` is the machinery for keeping it honest.
+
+## Decision
+
+**The encoder is hand-rolled, and every constant it writes with is re-derived from the official
+descriptors on a CI leg. Neither half ships without the other.**
+
+1. **Three layers, importing one way only.** `protobuf.rs` holds the wire primitives and knows
+   no field numbers; `perfetto_proto.rs` holds the field numbers and knows no wire format;
+   `perfetto.rs` writes messages out of both. The direction is what keeps the wire layer small
+   enough to audit against upstream, which is the reason for hand-rolling at all.
+2. **The field-number table and its proof are one declaration.** A macro in `perfetto_proto.rs`
+   emits each constant *and* its entry in the list handed to the checker, so a constant that
+   nothing asserts cannot be written. gcmon's equivalent is two files that a careless commit
+   can separate.
+3. **The checker is the harness's, not gcscope's.** `tests/harness/proto_constants.py` takes
+   `(message, field, number)` claims and answers from `perfetto_trace_pb2`. It knows nothing
+   about who is asking or what they intend to write, which is the same rule the dump harness
+   follows: reading `tests/harness/` should not reveal what gcscope emits.
+4. **Every primitive is decoded back by the `perfetto` package**, at the values where an
+   encoder goes wrong — the varint boundaries, a negative that a 32-bit mask changes, a double
+   whose bits are not its decimal, a string whose byte length is not its character count, an
+   empty submessage.
+5. **`perfetto` is a test dependency and never a runtime one.** Nothing under `src/` may import
+   a generated message class. A line such as `use perfetto_trace_pb2::CounterDescriptor` would
+   work, would be tempting, and would undo the decision.
+6. **Timestamps live on `TracePacket.timestamp`, and every packet names its sequence.** Two of
+   gcmon's four bugs are these two rules; they are in `perfetto_proto.rs`'s comments as well as
+   here.
+7. **`--output` names the Chrome path, and a format whose bytes are not JSON resolves its own.**
+   `--format perfetto -o run.json` writes `run.perfetto-trace`. `.json` is the one extension
+   replaced, because it is the one that would lie about the contents; any other suffix is
+   appended to, since `-o capture.2026-08-09` is a name an operator chose rather than a claim
+   about the format, and replacing it would fold two days' captures into one file. The
+   resolution happens in the fan-out rather than in each encoder, so two formats given one
+   `--output` write two files instead of truncating each other into one.
+
+## Consequences
+
+- gcscope gains no build-time codegen, no vendored `.proto` tree, and no serialization crate.
+  The `perfetto` package stays a `requirements.txt` line for one CI leg.
+- Upstream renumbering is caught by a test rather than by an operator, and it is one edit in one
+  file when it happens. It is caught only on the leg that has the package: a laptop running
+  `cargo test` sees the encoder's own unit tests and not the schema.
+- **The checker is only as current as the pinned `perfetto`.** `requirements.txt` pins it
+  exactly, so a field added or moved upstream is invisible until someone bumps the pin. That is
+  the same shape as the layout sweep in [ADR 0011](0011-layout-equivalence-sweep.md): the
+  guarantee is against the schema someone checked in, not against the world.
+- The pin is `0.57.2` rather than `0.56.0` because `TrackDescriptor.process_ordering` and
+  `thread_ordering` do not exist in the older schema, and a constant with nothing to check
+  against is a constant nobody is guarding.
+- A negative `int32` decodes the same whether it was sign-extended to ten bytes or truncated to
+  five, because the reader takes the low 32 bits either way. So the ten-byte form the spec asks
+  for is pinned by a unit test on the bytes, and the *value* assertions through the decoder
+  catch it only on an `int64` field. Both are kept; neither alone covers it.
+- A trace is the concatenation of its packets, with no header, length or index, so the encoder
+  appends as it goes and a capture killed mid-run leaves a readable prefix. Chrome's array
+  terminator has no counterpart here, which is why `close` only flushes.
+- The uuid-0 root descriptor is written on `open` rather than before the first event, so a run
+  that observed nothing still produces a file a reader opens.
+- Two formats now answer differently to the same `--output`, so the line a run prints names the
+  files it opened rather than the path that was typed.
+- The Perfetto output is pinned byte-for-byte the way the Chrome output is, at the bottom of
+  `exporters/perfetto.rs`. Ascending field order and a fixed sequence id are decisions, and
+  packet counts and length prefixes both survive breaking them.
+
+## Alternatives considered
+
+- **`prost` with Perfetto's `.proto` files.** Rejected for the dependency and the vendored
+  schema tree, given that the checker recovers most of the safety a generated encoder would
+  have. Worth revisiting if gcscope starts writing a substantially larger slice of the format,
+  or if interning arrives — that adds state the hand-rolled path would have to grow.
+- **Assert the field numbers in Rust against a copy of the schema.** A copy is the thing being
+  checked, so the test would agree with the table by construction. The numbers have to come
+  from outside the repo.
+- **Round-trip the encoder's output through a reader gcscope owns.** The failure this whole ADR
+  is about survives it: a wrong constant is read back through the same wrong constant. gcmon's
+  four bugs all passed their round-trip tests.

+# 0022 — Every timestamp gcscope writes names the clock it is on
+
+**Status:** Accepted — implemented 2026-08-09, with the first timestamp gcscope writes into a
+Perfetto trace. Extends [ADR 0017](0017-monitoring-tiers-follow-the-entry-layout.md)'s
+"absent rather than zero" from pause figures to timestamps.
+
+**Superseded in part by [ADR 0023](0023-one-clock-read-per-platform.md) (2026-08-12).** Decision 4
+below is discharged: the machine-readable declaration exists, so a trace may now carry Collections
+and gcscope's own markers together. Decision 1's `clock` debug annotation is **gone**, replaced by
+the domain on the packet. **Decision 3 is reversed** — the Observer's clock has no origin of its
+own any more, because it turned out not to be a clock of its own; see the note under it. Decision 2
+stands unchanged. The last consequence below — which predicted that the target's readings would
+have to become offsets into a domain gcscope invents — turned out to be wrong, and ADR 0023 says
+why it is left standing here rather than edited away.
+
+## Context
+
+A gcscope trace carries readings from two clocks, and nothing in it says so.
+
+- **The target's clock.** `ts_start`/`ts_stop` on a Record are what CPython published, from its
+  own monotonic counter. gcscope copies them through untouched — the raw numbers are what the
+  target said.
+- **The Observer's clock.** Nanoseconds since the run began, read from `Instant::now()` at each
+  poll. A build that publishes no timestamps has nothing else to place a counter sample on
+  ([ADR 0017](0017-monitoring-tiers-follow-the-entry-layout.md)), and so does anything gcscope
+  says about itself, such as when it attached to a process.
+
+The two share no origin. The Observer's starts near zero; the target's is a counter that has
+been running as long as the interpreter has. Put side by side with nothing distinguishing them,
+they read as one timeline and are decades apart on it. gcmon writes both into one trace and
+says nothing, which is the state this decision is against.
+
+Underneath it sits the older habit of writing `0` for a reading gcscope does not have.
+`mark_process_lifecycle` took a `ts_ns` that all three of its call sites passed `0` for. A zero
+is not "no value" — it is the origin, a point on the timeline like any other, and the only thing
+that distinguishes it from a measurement is knowing it was a placeholder.
+
+Perfetto has a mechanism for exactly this: `TracePacket.timestamp_clock_id`, with a
+`ClockSnapshot` correlating a producer's clock to a builtin one. **We tested it.** A custom
+clock domain works — trace-processor converts the events into trace time correctly — but only
+when the snapshot anchors it to **BOOTTIME**. Anchored to REALTIME or MONOTONIC instead,
+trace-processor reports `clock_sync_failure_no_path` and **drops the events entirely**.
+
+That is the mechanism gcscope wants and cannot reach yet, for two separate reasons:
+
+- Anchoring the Observer's clock needs a BOOTTIME reading. Rust's `Instant` deliberately exposes
+  no absolute value, so this means per-platform code — `CLOCK_BOOTTIME`, `GetTickCount64`,
+  `mach_continuous_time` — and a dependency to call it through.
+- Anchoring the **target's** clock is not a matter of effort. A snapshot pairs two clocks read
+  at one instant, and gcscope cannot read CPython's counter on demand; it sees only the values
+  already written into Records. There is no instant at which to take the pair.
+
+  *(This second point is where the reasoning went wrong, and
+  [ADR 0023](0023-one-clock-read-per-platform.md) is the correction: gcscope cannot read CPython's
+  counter, but it does not need to — the counter is a system clock, and gcscope can read that.)*
+
+## Decision
+
+1. **Every timestamp gcscope writes says which clock it came from.** Today that statement is a
+   `clock` debug annotation on the event carrying the timestamp, so it travels with the number
+   and is visible both in the UI and in trace-processor's `args`.
+2. **A reading gcscope does not have is absent, never zero.** `mark_process_lifecycle` takes an
+   `Option<i64>`; an encoder handed `None` writes no timestamp, and where the format needs one
+   to place an event, it writes no event. `ProcessDescriptor.start_timestamp_ns` is left off for
+   the same reason: it wants the moment the process began, on the target's clock, and gcscope
+   attached partway through a program already running.
+3. ~~**The Observer's clock keeps its origin at the attach.** It is what a run's counter samples
+   are already on, and a trace starting near zero reads more easily than one starting at
+   1.7×10¹⁸. Moving it to wall time to make the correlation easier would change every existing
+   counter-only trace for a benefit the correlation does not yet deliver.~~
+
+   **Reversed (2026-08-12), by the step that first drew counter tracks in a Perfetto trace.**
+   This reads as a choice about presentation and is not one. A build with no timestamps places its
+   samples on this reading and a build with timestamps places everything on the target's, so an
+   origin at the attach makes those two origins in one event stream, and nothing downstream can
+   tell which of them a `TraceEvent` carries. A tree holding a 3.13 target and a 3.15 one
+   described them decades apart in either format. Since
+   [ADR 0023](0023-one-clock-read-per-platform.md) the Observer's clock is *the machine's
+   monotonic clock*, so there is no origin left to choose: `MonitorContext::observed_at_ns` hands
+   over the poll's reading as it is, and every timestamp crossing the exporter boundary is in the
+   one domain. Traces do now start at 1.7×10¹⁸, which was the cost this decision declined to pay
+   for a benefit it could not yet see.
+4. **`timestamp_clock_id` + a BOOTTIME-anchored `ClockSnapshot` is the target state**, and it is
+   **required before a trace carries both clocks at once**. Perfetto traces at the time of writing
+   carried only Observer-clock events; the step that adds Collections adds target-clock ones, and
+   it inherits this. *(Discharged by ADR 0023, which also found that the two are one clock — so
+   what the declaration ended up carrying is the one domain both are in.)*
+
+## Consequences
+
+- A process gcscope watched appears in the trace with a marker saying when gcscope started
+  watching, and a reader who wonders what that number is relative to can find out from the
+  event itself.
+- The annotation is prose, not a clock domain. Trace-processor cannot use it to convert
+  anything, so a trace mixing both clocks would still render wrong — it would merely say so. The
+  rule in decision 4 exists because that is not good enough.
+- Whoever implements the machine-readable form pays for a portable boot-clock reading, and finds
+  that the target's clock still cannot be snapshotted. The likely shape is to declare the
+  Observer's clock properly and treat the target's readings as offsets into a domain gcscope
+  defines from the first Record it reads — which changes the numbers in the trace, so it is a
+  decision of its own rather than an implementation detail of this one.
+- gcscope now announces a process the moment it attaches rather than when the process first
+  collects. A worker that collected nothing reaches both exporters, so the Chrome trace gains a
+  `process_name` line it did not have.
+- **That does not finish the job on the Chrome side.** A Chrome trace holding only that
+  metadata line yields a `process` row and no track and no slice — checked, not assumed — for
+  the same reason the Perfetto UI hides an empty track. Perfetto's answer is the marker this
+  ADR times; Chrome's would be a `TraceEvent::Instant`, and the encoder can already write one
+  (`"ph":"I"`, process-scoped). It is not written, because it would put an event into every
+  Chrome trace an operator has ever captured and this decision is about clocks. So the silent
+  worker is visible in a Perfetto trace and still only in the process list of a Chrome one.

+# 0023 — The Observer's clock is the target's clock, read per platform
+
+**Status:** Accepted — implemented 2026-08-12, with the step that puts Collections in a Perfetto
+trace. Discharges decision 4 of [ADR 0022](0022-every-timestamp-names-its-clock.md), and replaces
+the shape that ADR predicted.
+
+## Context
+
+[ADR 0022](0022-every-timestamp-names-its-clock.md) left one thing undone and one thing
+forbidden. Undone: the machine-readable clock declaration, `timestamp_clock_id` with a
+`ClockSnapshot`. Forbidden: a trace holding both of gcscope's clocks until that existed. Adding
+Collections to a Perfetto trace runs straight into the second, because a Collection's timestamps
+are the target's and the marker beside it is gcscope's own.
+
+ADR 0022 also predicted what the fix would cost:
+
+> Whoever implements the machine-readable form pays for a portable boot-clock reading, and finds
+> that the target's clock still cannot be snapshotted. The likely shape is to declare the
+> Observer's clock properly and treat the target's readings as offsets into a domain gcscope
+> defines from the first Record it reads — which changes the numbers in the trace.
+
+The first half held. The second was wrong, and it was wrong in a way worth writing down, because
+the predicted shape would have been a **fabrication**: anchoring the target's clock to "the poll
+that first read a Record" claims a Collection happened when gcscope noticed it, and a ring at
+attach can hold Collections from an hour before. Every number in the trace would have moved by an
+unknown amount.
+
+**The two clocks were never two.** The Probe times a Collection with `PyTime_PerfCounterRaw`, and
+CPython's perf counter is the machine's monotonic counter — `CLOCK_MONOTONIC` on Linux,
+`mach_absolute_time` on macOS, `QueryPerformanceCounter` on Windows. Every one of those is
+system-wide. gcscope runs on the same machine, so it can read the very same counter in its own
+process and get a value in the same domain, exactly, with nothing to estimate. Rust's `Instant`
+hides its absolute value, which is what made this look impossible; a `clock_gettime` call does
+not.
+
+Measured on Windows before any of this was built: CPython reported `perf_counter_ns` =
+721728960985600 and gcscope read 721728960939900 a moment earlier — 46 ms apart, which is what it
+costs to spawn an interpreter.
+
+## Decision
+
+1. **gcscope reads the machine's monotonic clock itself** (`src/monitor/clock.rs`), per platform,
+   and that reading is the origin the Observer's clock counts from. There is one clock in a
+   gcscope trace, not two that have to be reconciled.
+2. **The numbers CPython published reach the trace unchanged.** No offsetting, no rebasing. A
+   Collection's `ts_start` in a Perfetto trace is the integer the target wrote, which is also what
+   the Chrome trace of the same run carries — so the two formats cannot come to disagree about
+   when something happened.
+3. **The trace declares that domain** rather than converting into one Perfetto already knows:
+   `timestamp_clock_id` on every packet carrying a timestamp, and one `ClockSnapshot` pairing the
+   domain with BOOTTIME. The conversion is the reader's, and the claim gcscope is making is
+   visible in the file.
+4. **Which system clock a platform's CPython uses is verified, not inferred.** It fails open in
+   exactly the way [ADR 0004](0004-per-platform-image-layout.md)'s image facts do — a wrong clock
+   returns a plausible number and the trace is merely wrong — so `live_smoke.rs` asks a real
+   interpreter for `time.perf_counter_ns()` and compares it against gcscope's own reading, on
+   every leg of the matrix.
+5. **The BOOTTIME anchor is read once, at the start of the run.** Re-anchoring mid-run would put
+   two disagreeing claims in one file.
+
+## Consequences
+
+- A Perfetto trace holds Collections and the markers gcscope puts beside them on one timeline,
+  and the operator who zooms into a pause sees the attach where it belongs rather than days away.
+- The `clock` debug annotation ADR 0022 introduced is **gone**. It said in prose what the domain
+  now says in a form trace-processor can act on, and a second statement that goes stale
+  independently of the first is worse than none.
+- **BOOTTIME is load-bearing and was tested twice.** ADR 0022 recorded that anchoring to REALTIME
+  or MONOTONIC makes trace-processor report `clock_sync_failure_no_path` and drop the events;
+  `tests/perfetto_encoder.rs` now fails that way on purpose if the constant is changed, so the
+  finding is a test rather than a paragraph.
+- **A machine that suspends mid-capture shifts the trace by the length of its nap.** BOOTTIME
+  counts through suspend and the monotonic clock does not, and the anchor between them is read
+  once. Nothing inside the trace moves relative to anything else, which is the property that
+  matters; what moves is where the whole trace sits against another producer's.
+- gcscope takes `libc` and `windows-sys` as direct dependencies. Both were already in the tree
+  through `remoteprocess` and friends, so this costs a manifest line rather than a build.
+- ~~The Observer's clock keeps its origin at the attach, so a counter-only trace on a build with
+  no timestamps is unchanged.~~ **This was wrong, and the step after this one found it.** A build
+  with no timestamps places its samples on the Observer's reading and one with timestamps places
+  everything on the target's, and a reading counted from the attach makes those two different
+  origins in one event stream, which nothing downstream can tell apart. A tree holding a 3.13
+  target and a 3.15 one described them decades apart, in whichever format was asked for. So
+  decision 1 is applied all the way: `MonitorContext` reads the machine's monotonic clock and
+  hands the reading over as it is, and **every timestamp crossing the exporter boundary is in the
+  one domain** — a Collection's, a counter sample's, a lifecycle mark's alike. Nothing counts
+  nanoseconds since the run began any more, and the rebase that did (`RunClock::observer_to_monotonic`)
+  is gone. The `--summary` figures are untouched; they were always differences.
+- A fourth Unix would compile with the anchor degraded to a single clock — internally exact,
+  absolutely unplaced. gcscope is built and tested on three.

@@ -0,0 +1,257 @@
+//! The machine's clocks, read the way CPython reads them.
+//!
+//! A gcscope trace carries readings from two sources
+//! ([ADR 0022](../../docs/adr/0022-every-timestamp-names-its-clock.md)): what CPython published
+//! on a Record, and what gcscope noted about itself. Until now those were two *domains* — the
+//! target's counter, and nanoseconds since the run began — sharing a trace and no origin, which
+//! is why nothing was allowed to hold both.
+//!
+//! This module collapses them into one, and the reason it can is that they were never really
+//! two. The Probe times a Collection with `PyTime_PerfCounterRaw`, and CPython's perf counter is
+//! the machine's monotonic clock: `CLOCK_MONOTONIC` on Linux, `mach_absolute_time` on macOS,
+//! `QueryPerformanceCounter` on Windows. Every one of those is **system-wide** — gcscope reads
+//! the same counter in its own process and gets a value in the same domain, exactly, with no
+//! correspondence to estimate. So the Observer's clock stops being a domain of its own: a reading
+//! gcscope takes of itself is a point on the target's timeline, and it is carried as one. Nothing
+//! anywhere counts nanoseconds since the run began, because a number like that needs a second
+//! origin to mean anything and this module is how the first one was removed.
+//!
+//! **Which clock a platform's CPython uses is a fact to verify, not to infer**, and it fails
+//! open exactly as the image-layout facts in
+//! [ADR 0004](../../docs/adr/0004-per-platform-image-layout.md) do: a wrong choice still reads a
+//! plausible number, and the trace is merely wrong by however far the two counters happen to sit
+//! apart. `tests/live_smoke.rs` holds the gate — it attaches to a real interpreter and checks a
+//! real Record's timestamp against [`monotonic_now_ns`] — and CI runs it on all three.
+//!
+//! ## Why a second clock as well
+//!
+//! Perfetto converts a trace into *trace time*, and its default is BOOTTIME. A domain that
+//! cannot be related to it is not merely unconverted: trace-processor reports
+//! `clock_sync_failure_no_path` and drops the events. So the anchor is a pair —
+//! [`RunClock::boottime_ns`] beside [`RunClock::monotonic_ns`], read back to back — and it is
+//! read once. The two differ by however long the machine has spent suspended, so a laptop that
+//! sleeps mid-capture shifts everything after it by the nap; nothing inside the trace moves
+//! relative to anything else, which is the property that matters, and the alternative is
+//! re-anchoring mid-run and asking a reader to believe two disagreeing claims.
+//!
+//! ## Why these calls do not fail
+//!
+//! Every read below is documented as infallible on the platforms gcscope supports:
+//! `clock_gettime` fails only on a clock id it does not know, `QueryPerformanceCounter` "does
+//! not fail on Windows XP or later", and `GetTickCount64` returns no error at all. They are
+//! spelled that way rather than as `Option`, because the alternative is a fallback branch that
+//! no test can reach and that would quietly write the trace this module exists to prevent.
+
+/// One reading of both clocks, taken back to back: what ties the domain every gcscope timestamp
+/// is in to the one Perfetto measures trace time in.
+///
+/// The pair is the point. Either reading alone says nothing — it is the two of them, at one
+/// instant, that let a reader convert. Without it a trace is still internally exact and merely
+/// floats, which trace-processor treats as unreadable rather than as unplaced.
+#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
+pub struct RunClock {
+    monotonic_ns: i64,
+    boottime_ns: u64,
+}
+
+impl RunClock {
+    /// Read both clocks now. Called once, when a run begins.
+    pub fn start() -> Self {
+        // Back to back and in this order, so the pair describes one instant as nearly as two
+        // reads can. Whatever gap is left shifts the whole trace by it and nothing within.
+        let monotonic_ns = monotonic_now_ns();
+        let boottime_ns = boottime_now_ns();
+        RunClock {
+            monotonic_ns,
+            boottime_ns,
+        }
+    }
+
+    /// A fixed anchor, for tests that pin bytes. A real one is two live readings, so a trace
+    /// built on one is never twice the same.
+    pub fn at(monotonic_ns: i64, boottime_ns: u64) -> Self {
+        RunClock {
+            monotonic_ns,
+            boottime_ns,
+        }
+    }
+
+    /// Where the run began on the machine's monotonic clock: the domain half of the pair the
+    /// clock snapshot publishes.
+    pub fn monotonic_ns(&self) -> i64 {
+        self.monotonic_ns
+    }
+
+    /// The same instant on Perfetto's trace clock.
+    pub fn boottime_ns(&self) -> u64 {
+        self.boottime_ns
+    }
+}
+
+/// When this process began monitoring, read once and shared.
+///
+/// One reading rather than one per caller. Every timestamp in a trace is read against this pair,
+/// so two anchors taken a few milliseconds apart would be two disagreeing claims about where the
+/// same trace sits. Whichever caller asks first fixes it.
+pub fn run_clock() -> RunClock {
+    static RUN: std::sync::OnceLock<RunClock> = std::sync::OnceLock::new();
+    *RUN.get_or_init(RunClock::start)
+}
+
+/// The machine's monotonic clock in nanoseconds — the counter CPython's perf counter reads, so
+/// a value from here and a Record's `ts_start` are two points on one timeline.
+pub fn monotonic_now_ns() -> i64 {
+    platform::monotonic_ns()
+}
+
+/// The same instant on a clock counting from boot and through suspend: Perfetto's trace clock.
+pub fn boottime_now_ns() -> u64 {
+    platform::boottime_ns()
+}
+
+#[cfg(unix)]
+mod platform {
+    /// macOS. CPython times with `mach_absolute_time`, and Darwin documents `CLOCK_UPTIME_RAW`
+    /// as that same counter already in nanoseconds — which is also why it is the *monotonic*
+    /// one here and `CLOCK_MONOTONIC` is the boot one: on Darwin the names are the other way
+    /// round from Linux's. `CLOCK_MONOTONIC` keeps counting while the machine sleeps;
+    /// `CLOCK_UPTIME_RAW` does not.
+    #[cfg(target_vendor = "apple")]
+    const MONOTONIC: libc::clockid_t = libc::CLOCK_UPTIME_RAW;
+    #[cfg(target_vendor = "apple")]
+    const BOOTTIME: libc::clockid_t = libc::CLOCK_MONOTONIC;
+
+    /// Linux, where CPython's perf counter is `clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC)` outright.
+    #[cfg(target_os = "linux")]
+    const MONOTONIC: libc::clockid_t = libc::CLOCK_MONOTONIC;
+    #[cfg(target_os = "linux")]
+    const BOOTTIME: libc::clockid_t = libc::CLOCK_BOOTTIME;
+
+    /// Any other Unix. gcscope is built and tested on three platforms; this keeps a fourth
+    /// compiling, with the anchor degraded to a single clock — the trace stays internally exact
+    /// and loses the suspend time that would have placed it correctly against other producers.
+    #[cfg(all(unix, not(target_vendor = "apple"), not(target_os = "linux")))]
+    const MONOTONIC: libc::clockid_t = libc::CLOCK_MONOTONIC;
+    #[cfg(all(unix, not(target_vendor = "apple"), not(target_os = "linux")))]
+    const BOOTTIME: libc::clockid_t = libc::CLOCK_MONOTONIC;
+
+    fn read(clock: libc::clockid_t) -> i128 {
+        // Zeroed rather than built from a literal: on some targets `timespec` carries private
+        // padding fields, and a struct literal does not compile there.
+        let mut ts: libc::timespec = unsafe { std::mem::zeroed() };
+        // Fails only on a clock id the kernel does not know, and both above are constants from
+        // the platform's own headers.
+        unsafe { libc::clock_gettime(clock, &mut ts) };
+        i128::from(ts.tv_sec) * 1_000_000_000 + i128::from(ts.tv_nsec)
+    }
+
+    pub(super) fn monotonic_ns() -> i64 {
+        read(MONOTONIC) as i64
+    }
+
+    pub(super) fn boottime_ns() -> u64 {
+        read(BOOTTIME).max(0) as u64
+    }
+}
+
+#[cfg(windows)]
+mod platform {
+    use windows_sys::Win32::System::Performance::{
+        QueryPerformanceCounter, QueryPerformanceFrequency,
+    };
+    use windows_sys::Win32::System::SystemInformation::GetTickCount64;
+
+    /// The performance counter in nanoseconds, the way CPython scales it.
+    ///
+    /// Whole seconds first and the remainder after, rather than `ticks * 1e9 / frequency`: the
+    /// counter is around 7×10¹⁴ on a machine up for a week, and multiplying that by a billion
+    /// overflows an `i64` in the first hour of uptime. The usual frequency is 10 MHz, where the
+    /// division is exact and this is `ticks * 100`.
+    pub(super) fn monotonic_ns() -> i64 {
+        let mut frequency = 0i64;
+        let mut ticks = 0i64;
+        // Neither fails on Windows XP or later, which Microsoft documents outright.
+        unsafe {
+            QueryPerformanceFrequency(&mut frequency);
+            QueryPerformanceCounter(&mut ticks);
+        }
+        if frequency <= 0 {
+            return 0;
+        }
+        (ticks / frequency) * 1_000_000_000 + (ticks % frequency) * 1_000_000_000 / frequency
+    }
+
+    /// Milliseconds since boot, suspend included, which is what Perfetto's BOOTTIME means. Its
+    /// resolution is the scheduler tick rather than the performance counter's, and that costs
+    /// the whole trace one uniform shift of up to ~16 ms — not one event its place beside
+    /// another.
+    pub(super) fn boottime_ns() -> u64 {
+        unsafe { GetTickCount64() }.saturating_mul(1_000_000)
+    }
+}
+
+#[cfg(test)]
+mod tests {
+    use super::*;
+
+    /// Both clocks read something a timeline can hold, and both move forwards. Thin, because
+    /// the claim that matters — that this is the counter CPython published — cannot be made
+    /// against gcscope's own process: it needs a live interpreter and a real Record, and that
+    /// test is in `tests/live_smoke.rs`.
+    #[test]
+    fn both_clocks_advance() {
+        let first = RunClock::start();
+        assert!(first.monotonic_ns() > 0, "{}", first.monotonic_ns());
+        assert!(first.boottime_ns() > 0, "{}", first.boottime_ns());
+
+        // Busy-wait rather than sleep: a sleep in a unit test is a slow test, and the counters
+        // move at nanosecond resolution on every platform here.
+        let started = std::time::Instant::now();
+        while started.elapsed() < std::time::Duration::from_millis(2) {
+            std::hint::spin_loop();
+        }
+
+        let second = RunClock::start();
+        assert!(
+            second.monotonic_ns() > first.monotonic_ns(),
+            "the monotonic clock stood still: {} then {}",
+            first.monotonic_ns(),
+            second.monotonic_ns()
+        );
+        assert!(second.boottime_ns() >= first.boottime_ns());
+    }
+
+    /// The two clocks are readings of one machine, so they cannot be eras apart. A pairing that
+    /// is (say) a monotonic counter beside a wall clock would show up here as the ~55 years
+    /// between the epoch and now, and nowhere else until a trace came out unreadable.
+    #[test]
+    fn the_pair_describes_one_machine() {
+        let clock = RunClock::start();
+        let monotonic = clock.monotonic_ns();
+        let boottime = clock.boottime_ns() as i64;
+        let apart = (boottime - monotonic).abs();
+        // A year of suspended time is far more than any real gap and far less than the
+        // difference a wrong clock would show.
+        assert!(
+            apart < 365 * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1_000_000_000i64,
+            "the clocks are {apart} ns apart: monotonic {monotonic}, boottime {boottime}"
+        );
+    }
+
+    /// One reading of this clock is what every timestamp gcscope writes is placed against, so
+    /// two callers asking must get the one instant rather than the two they happened to ask at.
+    ///
+    /// The wait is what makes this deterministic: two readings taken back to back could agree by
+    /// landing in one tick of the counter, and after two milliseconds they could not.
+    #[test]
+    fn the_runs_anchor_is_read_once_and_shared() {
+        let first = run_clock();
+
+        let started = std::time::Instant::now();
+        while started.elapsed() < std::time::Duration::from_millis(2) {
+            std::hint::spin_loop();
+        }
+
+        assert_eq!(run_clock(), first);
+    }
+}

+//! Fan one stream of [`TraceEvent`]s out to several formats.
+//!
+//! This is where the spec's rule lives in code: **an exporter encodes what it is handed and
+//! never converts from a Record itself**. Every member sees the same `&[TraceEvent]` slice,
+//! in the same order, so two formats cannot describe one run differently. gcmon reached that
+//! the expensive way — its Chrome and Perfetto paths each converted independently and drifted
+//! into two disagreeing traces of one run (gcmon ADR-0007).
+//!
+//! Metadata dedup stays inside each member rather than here. It is a property of one output
+//! stream: two formats fanned out from one conversion each need their own copy of a
+//! `process_name`, and a combiner that dropped the second would leave the second format's
+//! track unnamed.
+
+use std::path::{Path, PathBuf};
+
+use super::{EventsExporter, ProcessLifecycle};
+use crate::monitor::trace_event::TraceEvent;
+
+/// Several [`EventsExporter`]s driven as one.
+///
+/// ## What a failing member does to the others
+///
+/// The two fallible calls answer differently, because the cost of carrying on differs:
+///
+/// - **`open` is all-or-nothing.** An operator who asked for two formats and silently got one
+///   would find out when they went looking for the file. On the first member that fails, the
+///   members already opened are closed — each left a valid, if empty, trace rather than a
+///   half-written one — and the error is returned, so the run never starts.
+/// - **`close` closes every member even after one fails**, and reports the first error. A
+///   skipped `close` is what leaves a format's file unterminated: Chrome's array is closed
+///   there, so returning early on the first error would corrupt the very traces the run was
+///   for.
+///
+/// ## One `--output`, one file per member
+///
+/// Every member is asked where it writes ([`EventsExporter::output_path`]) before it is
+/// opened, so two formats given one `--output` land in two files rather than truncating each
+/// other into one. The rule is applied here rather than inside each encoder, because it is a
+/// property of the composition: an encoder used alone still writes exactly where it is told.
+///
+/// No `Default`. An empty fan-out opens, closes and swallows every batch without error, so a
+/// run would report a trace written to a file that was never created. The only constructor
+/// takes its members.
+pub struct CombiningExporter {
+    members: Vec<Box<dyn EventsExporter>>,
+    /// What the last [`open`](EventsExporter::open) resolved to, in member order. Recorded on
+    /// the way through rather than recomputed, so the run reports the files it opened.
+    opened: Vec<PathBuf>,
+}
+
+impl CombiningExporter {
+    pub fn new(members: Vec<Box<dyn EventsExporter>>) -> Self {
+        Self {
+            members,
+            opened: Vec::new(),
+        }
+    }
+
+    /// The files this fan-out opened, in member order. Empty before the first `open`.
+    pub fn opened_paths(&self) -> &[PathBuf] {
+        &self.opened
+    }
+}
+
+impl EventsExporter for CombiningExporter {
+    fn open(&mut self, path: &Path) -> std::io::Result<()> {
+        self.opened.clear();
+        for index in 0..self.members.len() {
+            let resolved = self.members[index].output_path(path);
+            if let Err(error) = self.members[index].open(&resolved) {
+                for opened in &mut self.members[..index] {
+                    let _ = opened.close();
+                }
+                self.opened.clear();
+                return Err(error);
+            }
+            self.opened.push(resolved);
+        }
+        Ok(())
+    }
+
+    fn add_events(&mut self, events: &[TraceEvent]) {
+        for member in &mut self.members {
+            member.add_events(events);
+        }
+    }
+
+    fn mark_process_lifecycle(&mut self, pid: u32, kind: ProcessLifecycle, ts_ns: Option<i64>) {
+        for member in &mut self.members {
+            member.mark_process_lifecycle(pid, kind, ts_ns);
+        }
+    }
+
+    fn close(&mut self) -> std::io::Result<()> {
+        let mut first_error = None;
+        for member in &mut self.members {
+            if let Err(error) = member.close()
+                && first_error.is_none()
+            {
+                first_error = Some(error);
+            }
+        }
+        match first_error {
+            Some(error) => Err(error),
+            None => Ok(()),
+        }
+    }
+}

+    }
