+//! Argument handling that has to be true before anything is attached to or spawned.
+//!
+//! Unlike the rest of `tests/`, nothing here needs a Python interpreter or ptrace: it runs the
+//! gcscope binary with arguments it must refuse, and asserts it refused. So these are not
+//! `#[ignore]`d — they run in the default `cargo test`.
+
+use std::path::PathBuf;
+use std::process::Command;
+
+/// Run the gcscope binary, returning `(exit code, stdout, stderr)`. The two streams stay
+/// apart: clap prints a refusal on stderr and `--help` on stdout, and each test asserts on
+/// the one that matters.
+fn gcscope(args: &[&str]) -> (i32, String, String) {
+    let out = Command::new(env!("CARGO_BIN_EXE_gcscope"))
+        .args(args)
+        .output()
+        .expect("spawn gcscope");
+    (
+        out.status.code().unwrap_or(-1),
+        String::from_utf8_lossy(&out.stdout).into_owned(),
+        String::from_utf8_lossy(&out.stderr).into_owned(),
+    )
+}
+
+fn temp_path(tag: &str) -> PathBuf {
+    std::env::temp_dir().join(format!("gcscope_cli_{}_{}.json", std::process::id(), tag))
+}
+
+/// A format gcscope does not have is refused with the list of the ones it does, and refused
+/// early enough that no target was touched. `monitor` names a PID that may well exist; the
+/// point is that the run never gets far enough to care.
+#[test]
+fn an_unrecognised_format_is_refused_with_the_accepted_list() {
+    for args in [
+        vec!["monitor", "1234", "--format", "perfetto-ish"],
+        vec![
+            "run",
+            "-p",
+            "python",
+            "-s",
+            "spin.py",
+            "--format",
+            "perfetto-ish",
+        ],
+    ] {
+        let (code, _, stderr) = gcscope(&args);
+        assert_ne!(code, 0, "{args:?} was accepted\n{stderr}");
+        assert!(
+            stderr.contains("perfetto-ish"),
+            "the refusal does not say what was rejected: {stderr}"
+        );
+        assert!(
+            stderr.contains("chrome"),
+            "the refusal does not name what is accepted: {stderr}"
+        );
+    }
+}
+
+/// The refusal happens before the output path is opened, so a bad `--format` cannot cost an
+/// operator the trace already sitting there — nor leave an empty file where there was none.
+#[test]
+fn an_unrecognised_format_neither_creates_nor_truncates_the_output_file() {
+    let existing = temp_path("existing");
+    let absent = temp_path("absent");
+    std::fs::write(&existing, "an earlier run's trace").unwrap();
+    std::fs::remove_file(&absent).ok();
+
+    for path in [&existing, &absent] {
+        let (code, _, stderr) = gcscope(&[
+            "monitor",
+            "1234",
+            "-o",
+            &path.to_string_lossy(),
+            "--format",
+            "perfetto-ish",
+        ]);
+        assert_ne!(code, 0, "{stderr}");
+    }
+
+    assert_eq!(
+        std::fs::read_to_string(&existing).unwrap(),
+        "an earlier run's trace"
+    );
+    assert!(!absent.exists(), "an empty trace was left behind");
+    std::fs::remove_file(&existing).ok();
+}
+
+/// The flag is optional and the default is the format that shipped before it existed, so an
+/// operator's existing command line means what it meant. `--help` is the cheapest place to
+/// read that back, and it is also where the accepted values are documented.
+#[test]
+fn help_documents_the_flag_its_default_and_its_values() {
+    for subcommand in ["monitor", "run"] {
+        let (code, help, stderr) = gcscope(&[subcommand, "--help"]);
+        assert_eq!(code, 0, "{stderr}");
+        assert!(help.contains("--format"), "{subcommand}: {help}");
+        assert!(help.contains("[default: chrome]"), "{subcommand}: {help}");
+    }
+}
+
+/// One `--output`, and a format whose bytes are not what that path's extension claims. Where
+/// the file actually lands is the operator's to know before the run, not after it, so `--help`
+/// carries the rule and this asserts the sentence is still there.
+///
+/// Compared against the help with its whitespace collapsed: clap wraps to the terminal width,
+/// so the sentence is one line here and two on a narrower one.
+#[test]
+fn help_says_where_a_perfetto_trace_lands() {
+    for subcommand in ["monitor", "run"] {
+        let (code, help, stderr) = gcscope(&[subcommand, "--help"]);
+        assert_eq!(code, 0, "{stderr}");
+
+        let unwrapped = help.split_whitespace().collect::<Vec<_>>().join(" ");
+        assert!(
+            unwrapped.contains("`--format perfetto -o run.json` writes `run.perfetto-trace`"),
+            "{subcommand}: {help}"
+        );
+    }
+}

+//! Run `tests/harness/perfetto_dump.py` and hand back the document it printed, parsed.
+//!
+//! The process boundary and the parsing are solved once, here, so a test asserting about a
+//! trace writes about the trace. The document's shape is the harness's to define; this side
+//! only runs it and hands back `serde_json::Value`.
+//!
+//! Why a real parser rather than the shell-out-and-print-lines pattern the live tests use: the
+//! question these tests ask is often "does the trace carry *exactly* these keys and no others",
+//! and a flat text protocol answers it by substring match, which passes whether or not the
+//! surprise was there. A key set is the assertion; a parsed document is what makes it one.
+
+// Each test binary compiles its own copy of `common`, so a helper only some of them use looks
+// unused in the others.
+#![allow(dead_code)]
+
+use std::io::Write;
+use std::path::{Path, PathBuf};
+use std::process::{Command, Stdio};
+
+use serde_json::Value;
+
+use super::test_python;
+
+/// The document version this helper reads. `perfetto_dump.py` publishes it under `schema`, and
+/// bumping it there without bumping it here is meant to fail loudly.
+const SCHEMA: &str = "gcscope.perfetto-dump/1";
+
+/// The same, for the field-number checker, which speaks a document of its own.
+const CONSTANTS_SCHEMA: &str = "gcscope.proto-constants/1";
+
+/// What the harness printed and what it concluded.
+pub struct Dump {
+    /// The parsed document. See `tests/harness/README.md` for its keys.
+    pub document: Value,
+    /// 0 the trace is structurally valid, 1 it is not. A harness failure never gets this far —
+    /// [`dump`] panics on one, since it means the test could not be run rather than that the
+    /// trace was bad.
+    pub exit_code: i32,
+}
+
+impl Dump {
+    /// The packets of the wire view. Panics if the bytes did not parse as a trace, which is a
+    /// separate failure from an invalid one and worth a different message.
+    pub fn packets(&self) -> &Vec<Value> {
+        self.document["wire"]["packet"]
+            .as_array()
+            .unwrap_or_else(|| panic!("the trace did not parse:\n{}", self.problems()))
+    }
+
+    /// The rows of one trace-processor query, by the name the harness gave it.
+    pub fn rows(&self, view: &str) -> &Vec<Value> {
+        let value = &self.document["trace_processor"][view];
+        value.as_array().unwrap_or_else(|| {
+            panic!("no `{view}` rows; the harness said: {value}. Did you skip the query engine?")
+        })
+    }
+
+    pub fn is_valid(&self) -> bool {
+        self.document["validity"]["ok"] == Value::Bool(true)
+    }
+
+    /// Every structural problem, one per line, for an assertion message.
+    pub fn problems(&self) -> String {
+        match self.document["validity"]["problems"].as_array() {
+            Some(problems) if !problems.is_empty() => problems
+                .iter()
+                .map(|p| format!("  {} — {}", p["check"], p["detail"]))
+                .collect::<Vec<_>>()
+                .join("\n"),
+            _ => "  (none)".to_string(),
+        }
+    }
+}
+
+/// The keys of one JSON object, sorted. What an "and nothing else" assertion compares — the
+/// question a text dump cannot answer, since an unexpected field is a token nobody read.
+pub fn keys(value: &Value) -> Vec<&str> {
+    let mut names: Vec<&str> = value
+        .as_object()
+        .unwrap_or_else(|| panic!("not an object: {value}"))
+        .keys()
+        .map(String::as_str)
+        .collect();
+    names.sort_unstable();
+    names
+}
+
+fn harness_dir() -> PathBuf {
+    Path::new(env!("CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR"))
+        .join("tests")
+        .join("harness")
+}
+
+fn harness_script() -> PathBuf {
+    harness_dir().join("perfetto_dump.py")
+}
+
+/// Write one of `reference_traces.py`'s traces to `out` and return the path.
+///
+/// These are authored with the protobuf bindings, so a decoder checked against them has been
+/// shown a trace this repo did not encode. `kind` is a name from that file's `TRACES`.
+pub fn reference_trace(python: &Path, kind: &str, out: &Path) -> PathBuf {
+    let status = Command::new(python)
+        .arg(harness_dir().join("reference_traces.py"))
+        .arg(kind)
+        .arg(out)
+        .output()
+        .expect("build a reference trace");
+    assert!(
+        status.status.success(),
+        "could not build the `{kind}` trace: {}",
+        String::from_utf8_lossy(&status.stderr)
+    );
+    out.to_path_buf()
+}
+
+/// An interpreter that can run the harness, or `None`.
+///
+/// It calls into the package rather than importing the name: `import perfetto` succeeds on the
+/// protobuf half alone, and a test that needs the query engine would then fail deep inside the
+/// harness instead of skipping here.
+pub fn harness_python() -> Option<PathBuf> {
+    let python = test_python()?;
+    let ok = Command::new(&python)
+        .args([
+            "-c",
+            "from perfetto.protos.perfetto.trace.perfetto_trace_pb2 import Trace; Trace()",
+        ])
+        .output()
+        .map(|out| out.status.success())
+        .unwrap_or(false);
+    ok.then_some(python)
+}
+
+/// Whether a missing `perfetto` package must **fail** rather than skip.
+///
+/// Skipping is right on a laptop and wrong on the leg that just installed the package, where it
+/// would turn a failed install into a green run. That leg sets `GCSCOPE_REQUIRE_PERFETTO=1`.
+pub fn perfetto_required() -> bool {
+    std::env::var("GCSCOPE_REQUIRE_PERFETTO").ok().as_deref() == Some("1")
+}
+
+/// An interpreter that can run the harness, or `None` after logging a skip.
+pub fn harness_python_or_skip(test: &str) -> Option<PathBuf> {
+    if let Some(python) = harness_python() {
+        return Some(python);
+    }
+    let msg = "no interpreter with the `perfetto` package \
+               (install it: pip install -r tests/harness/requirements.txt)";
+    assert!(
+        !perfetto_required(),
+        "GCSCOPE_REQUIRE_PERFETTO=1 but {msg}; a leg that installs it must not pass by skipping"
+    );
+    eprintln!("SKIP {test}: {msg}");
+    None
+}
+
+/// Hand a claims document to `proto_constants.py` and give back the verdict it printed.
+///
+/// The claims go over stdin rather than through a file: the table being checked is compiled
+/// into this test binary, so writing it out somewhere would only add a path to clean up.
+pub fn check_constants(python: &Path, claims: &str) -> Value {
+    let mut child = Command::new(python)
+        .arg(harness_dir().join("proto_constants.py"))
+        .arg("-")
+        .stdin(Stdio::piped())
+        .stdout(Stdio::piped())
+        .stderr(Stdio::piped())
+        .spawn()
+        .expect("run the constants checker");
+    child
+        .stdin
+        .take()
+        .expect("the checker reads stdin")
+        .write_all(claims.as_bytes())
+        .expect("hand over the claims");
+
+    let out = child.wait_with_output().expect("the checker finishes");
+    let stderr = String::from_utf8_lossy(&out.stderr);
+    assert_ne!(
+        out.status.code().unwrap_or(-1),
+        2,
+        "the checker could not run: {stderr}"
+    );
+
+    let stdout = String::from_utf8_lossy(&out.stdout);
+    let verdict: Value = serde_json::from_str(&stdout).unwrap_or_else(|e| {
+        panic!("the checker printed something that is not JSON: {e}\nstdout: {stdout}\nstderr: {stderr}")
+    });
+    assert_eq!(
+        verdict["schema"], CONSTANTS_SCHEMA,
+        "the checker speaks a document version this helper does not: {}",
+        verdict["schema"]
+    );
+    verdict
+}
+
+/// Both views of `trace`. Starts the query engine, which downloads its binary on first use.
+pub fn dump(python: &Path, trace: &Path) -> Dump {
+    run(python, trace, false)
+}
+
+/// The wire view alone — no query engine, so no download and no second process.
+pub fn dump_wire_only(python: &Path, trace: &Path) -> Dump {
+    run(python, trace, true)
+}
+
+fn run(python: &Path, trace: &Path, skip_trace_processor: bool) -> Dump {
+    let mut command = Command::new(python);
+    command.arg(harness_script()).arg(trace);
+    if skip_trace_processor {
+        command.arg("--skip-trace-processor");
+    }
+
+    let out = command.output().expect("run the dump harness");
+    let stderr = String::from_utf8_lossy(&out.stderr);
+    let code = out.status.code().unwrap_or(-1);
+
+    // 2 is the harness saying it could not run at all. That is this test's problem, not the
+    // trace's, and swallowing it would look like a trace with no packets.
+    assert_ne!(
+        code,
+        2,
+        "the harness could not read {}: {stderr}",
+        trace.display()
+    );
+
+    let stdout = String::from_utf8_lossy(&out.stdout);
+    let document: Value = serde_json::from_str(&stdout).unwrap_or_else(|e| {
+        panic!("the harness printed something that is not JSON: {e}\nstdout: {stdout}\nstderr: {stderr}")
+    });
+
+    // The harness versions its document for a reason, so read it. Without this, a harness that
+    // moved a key answers `Value::Null` to every lookup and the failure surfaces as
+    // "the trace did not parse" with an empty problem list — a test blaming the trace for a
+    // mismatch between these two files.
+    assert_eq!(
+        document["schema"], SCHEMA,
+        "the harness speaks a document version this helper does not: {}",
+        document["schema"]
+    );
+
+    Dump {
+        document,
+        exit_code: code,
+    }
+}

+# The Perfetto verification harness
+
+`perfetto_dump.py` reads a Perfetto trace and prints what is in it, as JSON, for another test
+to assert on. It exists because a hand-rolled protobuf encoder fails **open**: without a
+decoder gcscope did not write, a wrong field number produces a file that parses *to something
+else* rather than a file that does not parse — the failure mode
+[ADR 0004](../../docs/adr/0004-per-platform-image-layout.md) warns about.
+
+The harness is a translator, not a judge of content. It knows the Perfetto format; it knows
+nothing about GC. What tracks should exist, what a slice should be called, which counters
+should share an axis — those are expectations, and they live in Rust beside the encoder that
+produced them. **Reading this directory should not reveal what gcscope emits.**
+
+## Running it
+
+```powershell
+pip install -r tests/harness/requirements.txt
+
+# the harness itself
+python -m pytest tests/harness
+python -m pytest tests/harness -m "not trace_processor"   # skip the query engine
+
+# on a trace
+python tests/harness/perfetto_dump.py trace.perfetto-trace
+python tests/harness/perfetto_dump.py trace.perfetto-trace --skip-trace-processor
+
+# on a table of field numbers
+python tests/harness/proto_constants.py claims.json
+
+# from Rust
+cargo test --test perfetto_harness -- --ignored     # the seam
+cargo test --test perfetto_encoder -- --ignored     # gcscope's encoder through it
+```
+
+Rust reaches it through `tests/common/perfetto.rs`, which runs the script and hands back the
+parsed document. That module is the seam later Perfetto tests assert through, so nobody
+re-solves the process boundary or the parsing.
+
+## The document
+
+```json
+{
+  "schema": "gcscope.perfetto-dump/1",
+  "bytes": 412,
+  "validity": {"ok": false, "problems": [{"check": "…", "detail": "…", "packet": 4}]},
+  "wire": {"packet": [ … ]},
+  "trace_processor": {"slice": [ … ], "process": [ … ], "track": {"error": "…"}}
+}
+```
+
+`wire` is `null` when the bytes did not parse. `trace_processor` is `null` when the query
+engine was skipped, and any single query that fails becomes `{"error": …}` under its own name
+rather than taking the dump down — trace-processor's columns move between releases, and a
+caller that asked about slices should still get them on the day the `track` schema changes.
+The failure is in the document, so nobody mistakes a missing view for an empty one.
+
+Exit codes: **0** the trace is structurally valid, **1** it is not, **2** the harness could not
+run. A rejection is data either way, printed with its problems listed.
+
+## Three readers
+
+| reader | from | answers |
+|---|---|---|
+| `wire` | `perfetto_trace_pb2` | is this the field I meant to write |
+| `trace_processor` | the binary the Perfetto UI runs | does a wire-valid trace *mean* what it should |
+| `proto_constants.py` | the same generated descriptors | is this the number that field actually has |
+
+Fields the trace processor does not expose as columns — `sibling_order_rank` and
+`y_axis_share_key` among them — come from the wire view. Do not "fix" a missing column by
+asserting on something else that happens to exist.
+
+`counter_track_y_axis` is the shape that rule takes when a column might arrive: a query of its
+own, so its failure is one view's rather than `counter_track`'s, standing so that the day
+trace-processor models `y_axis_share_key` it starts answering and nobody has to remember to ask.
+It reads `{"error": …}` on 0.57.2.
+
+`proto_constants.py` is the narrowest of the three, and the only one that reads no trace. It
+takes claims — `(message, field, number)` and `(scope, enum, value, number)` — from a file or
+stdin, and answers whether the schema agrees, so a table of field numbers transcribed by hand
+in another language is re-derived from the descriptors on every run. It knows nothing about who
+is asking or what they intend to write into those fields. Same exit codes: **0** every claim
+holds, **1** at least one does not, **2** it could not run.
+
+A message is named by its path from the file, so a nested one is `ClockSnapshot.Clock` and the
+bare `Clock` stays unknown — resolving it by hunting through every parent would answer a question
+nobody asked. An enum the file declares outside any message, `BuiltinClock` among them, takes the
+empty scope `""`.
+
+Its answer is only as current as the pinned `perfetto`. A field added or moved upstream is
+invisible here until someone bumps `requirements.txt` — the guarantee is against the schema
+someone checked in, not against the world.
+
+## Three rendering decisions
+
+`MessageToDict` supplies the rendering, so the grammar comes from the `.proto` rather than from
+us. Three of its behaviours are decisions, each silent when wrong, each with a test in
+`test_perfetto_dump.py`:
+
+1. **`preserving_proto_field_name=True`.** Names arrive as the schema spells them. Without it
+   every name is camelCased and stops matching the field table an encoder was written against.
+2. **`always_print_fields_with_no_presence=False`.** A field nobody wrote stays absent. The
+   alternative prints every unwritten field at its default, drowning the one signal this view
+   is for — a producer wrote something nobody expected — in zeros it did not write. Safe here
+   in a way it would not be under proto3 defaults: Perfetto's fields carry explicit presence,
+   so a `0` that was written is rendered and a field never touched is omitted.
+3. **64-bit fields render as JSON strings.** Protobuf's rule rather than a choice, and the
+   right one: a nanosecond timestamp is around 1.7×10¹⁸ and an IEEE double holds integers
+   exactly only to 9×10¹⁵. Callers parse them from strings.
+
+## Structural checks
+
+Each check names itself in the problem it reports, so a caller asserts on the name rather than
+on the wording of a message. Every one has a test with a hand-built trace it must reject.
+
+| check | rule |
+|---|---|
+| `parses` | the bytes decode as a `Trace` |
+| `sequence_id` | every packet names the sequence it belongs to |
+| `track_uuid` | every track a `TrackEvent` names was declared by some `TrackDescriptor` |
+| `slice_pairing` | on each track, every begin closes and no end arrives unopened |
+
+`sequence_id` is stricter than the format demands — Perfetto tolerates packets outside any
+sequence. Interning and incremental state are sequence-scoped, so a packet that escapes its
+sequence is far more likely a producer bug than a design, and a producer that genuinely needs
+one should be made to say so here. `track_uuid` resolves a declaration made *anywhere* in the
+trace, since descriptors and events may be interleaved.
+
+Both track checks resolve **per-sequence defaults**: a producer may state
+`trace_packet_defaults.track_event_defaults.track_uuid` once and leave the field off every
+event after it, which is Perfetto's standard way of not repeating a uuid on thousands of
+packets. Reading only the explicit field calls that pattern malformed, and files every such
+event under track `0`, where a begin on one track pairs with an end on another — so the pairing
+check would go quiet exactly where it matters. Defaults hold until the sequence states new
+ones; `previous_packet_dropped` resetting them is not modelled.
+
+## Reference traces
+
+`reference_traces.py` builds them with the protobuf bindings, at call time rather than as
+committed bytes, so the reference and the schema cannot drift apart on disk. A decoder whose
+only input has ever been the encoder it checks is a weak oracle: the two agree by construction
+and neither has been shown a third opinion.
+
+None of them is a GC trace. The well-formed one is a process running a slice called `Work` with
+a `Detail` inside it and a counter that samples twice. The rest are the malformed cases the
+checks above must reject — a validity check nobody has watched reject something is a check that
+might only ever say yes.
+
+## Why the dependencies live here
+
+`requirements.txt` pins them exactly. The trace bytes do not depend on which interpreter a
+target runs, so this gains nothing from a range and loses reproducibility.
+
+They are deliberately **not** in `gcscope_probe/pyproject.toml`. That package is a distributable
+C extension whose `requires-python = ">=3.13,<3.15"` is an ABI gate on internal struct layout;
+a harness that reads a file format has no business inheriting an interpreter bound from it.

@@ -0,0 +1,352 @@
+"""Read a Perfetto trace and print what is in it, as JSON, for another test to assert on.
+
+This is a translator, not a judge of content. It knows the Perfetto *format* — that a
+`TrackEvent` must name a track someone declared, that a slice that opens must close — and
+nothing about what any particular producer writes. What tracks should exist, what a slice
+should be called, which counters should share an axis: those are expectations, and they belong
+in the test suite of whatever wrote the trace. Nothing in this file should reveal what gcscope
+emits.
+
+Two decoders, because they answer different questions:
+
+* **the wire view** (`perfetto_trace_pb2`) is the only thing that catches a field number wrong
+  from the first commit — a hand-rolled encoder that writes a string into the wrong field
+  produces bytes that parse *to something else*, not bytes that fail to parse.
+* **the trace-processor view** is the same binary the Perfetto UI runs, so it settles whether a
+  wire-valid trace *means* what it should.
+
+One document carries both, and the caller picks the one its question needs.
+
+Usage:
+    python perfetto_dump.py TRACE [--skip-trace-processor]
+
+Exit codes: 0 the trace is structurally valid, 1 it is not, 2 the harness could not run (bad
+arguments, unreadable file, missing dependency). A rejection is data either way — the document
+is printed on stdout with its problems listed, so a caller reads *what* was wrong rather than
+inferring it from a number.
+"""
+
+from __future__ import annotations
+
+import argparse
+import json
+import sys
+import traceback
+from pathlib import Path
+
+SCHEMA = "gcscope.perfetto-dump/1"
+
+# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
+# How the wire view is rendered
+# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
+
+# `MessageToDict` takes the grammar from the `.proto` rather than from us, which is the point:
+# a rendering this file invented would be one more thing to keep in step with the schema. Three
+# of its behaviours are decisions, though, and each is silent when wrong.
+RENDERING = {
+    # Names arrive as the schema spells them. Without this every name is camelCased, and stops
+    # matching the field table an encoder was written against.
+    "preserving_proto_field_name": True,
+    # A field nobody wrote stays absent. The alternative prints every unwritten field at its
+    # default, which would drown the one signal a reader wants from this view — that a producer
+    # wrote something nobody expected — in a hundred zeros it did not write.
+    #
+    # This is safe here in a way it would not be under proto3 defaults: Perfetto's fields carry
+    # explicit presence, so a `0` that was *written* is rendered and a field that was never
+    # touched is omitted. The two are distinguishable, and `test_perfetto_dump.py` pins that.
+    "always_print_fields_with_no_presence": False,
+}
+
+# 64-bit fields render as JSON *strings*, which is protobuf's rule rather than a choice, and it
+# is the correct one: a nanosecond timestamp is around 1.7e18 and an IEEE double holds integers
+# exactly only to 9e15. A caller parses them from strings. Pinned by a test, since a future
+# protobuf that "helpfully" emitted numbers would silently start rounding timestamps.
+
+# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
+# The trace-processor view
+# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
+
+# Every query is ordered, so two runs over one trace produce the same rows in the same
+# sequence. Without an ORDER BY, SQLite is free to return them however it likes.
+QUERIES = {
+    "slice": """
+        select id, ts, dur, track_id, depth, parent_id, category, name, arg_set_id
+        from slice order by ts, track_id, depth, id
+    """,
+    "slice_args": """
+        select s.id as slice_id, a.key, a.value_type, a.int_value, a.string_value, a.real_value
+        from slice s join args a on s.arg_set_id = a.arg_set_id
+        order by s.id, a.key
+    """,
+    "track": "select id, name, parent_id from track order by id",
+    "counter_track": "select id, name, parent_id, unit from counter_track order by id",
+    # A view of its own, because it is the one this release cannot answer. `y_axis_share_key` is
+    # a rendering hint rather than a property the query engine models, and there is no column for
+    # it as of 0.57.2 — so this lands as `{"error": ...}` and a caller reads why. Kept beside the
+    # others rather than deleted: the day the column arrives it starts answering, and nobody has
+    # to remember to ask again. Folding it into `counter_track` above would take that view down
+    # with it. A caller wanting the value today reads the wire view.
+    "counter_track_y_axis": "select id, name, y_axis_share_key from counter_track order by id",
+    "counter": "select id, ts, track_id, value from counter order by ts, track_id, id",
+    "process": "select upid, pid, name from process order by pid, upid",
+    "thread": "select utid, tid, name, upid from thread order by tid, utid",
+}
+
+
+def trace_processor_view(path: Path) -> dict:
+    """Run every query and return `{name: [row, ...]}`.
+
+    A query that fails becomes `{"error": ...}` under its own name rather than taking the whole
+    dump down. Trace-processor's columns move between releases, and a caller that asked about
+    slices should still get them on the day the `track` schema changes underneath it. The
+    failure is in the document, so nobody mistakes a missing view for an empty one.
+    """
+    from perfetto.trace_processor import TraceProcessor
+
+    view: dict[str, object] = {}
+    processor = TraceProcessor(trace=str(path))
+    try:
+        for name, sql in QUERIES.items():
+            try:
+                view[name] = [_row_as_dict(row) for row in processor.query(sql)]
+            except Exception as failure:  # noqa: BLE001 - reported, not handled
+                view[name] = {"error": f"{type(failure).__name__}: {failure}"}
+    finally:
+        processor.close()
+    return view
+
+
+def _row_as_dict(row) -> dict:
+    """One query result row as plain JSON values.
+
+    Trace-processor hands back a row object whose attributes are the selected columns; a NULL
+    arrives as `None` and stays `None`, since "this column had no value" is exactly what a
+    caller needs to tell apart from zero.
+    """
+    return {name: _json_safe(value) for name, value in vars(row).items()}
+
+
+def _json_safe(value):
+    if value is None or isinstance(value, (bool, int, float, str)):
+        return value
+    return str(value)
+
+
+# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
+# Structural validity
+# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
+
+
+def _problem(check: str, detail: str, packet: int | None = None) -> dict:
+    return {"check": check, "detail": detail, "packet": packet}
+
+
+def _effective_track_uuids(trace) -> list[int | None]:
+    """The track each packet's `TrackEvent` sits on, one entry per packet.
+
+    `None` for a packet that carries no event, and for an event whose track cannot be resolved.
+
+    A producer may state `trace_packet_defaults.track_event_defaults.track_uuid` once and leave
+    the field off every event after it — that is Perfetto's standard way of not repeating a
+    uuid on thousands of packets, and both spellings mean the same track. A checker reading
+    only the explicit field calls that pattern malformed, and worse, files every such event
+    under track `0`, so a begin on one track pairs with an end on another.
+
+    Defaults are per sequence and hold until that sequence states new ones. This does not model
+    `previous_packet_dropped` resetting them; a trace that needs it can say so here.
+    """
+    defaults: dict[int, int] = {}
+    resolved: list[int | None] = []
+    for packet in trace.packet:
+        sequence = packet.trusted_packet_sequence_id
+        if packet.HasField("trace_packet_defaults"):
+            event_defaults = packet.trace_packet_defaults.track_event_defaults
+            if event_defaults.HasField("track_uuid"):
+                defaults[sequence] = event_defaults.track_uuid
+
+        if packet.WhichOneof("data") != "track_event":
+            resolved.append(None)
+        elif packet.track_event.HasField("track_uuid"):
+            resolved.append(packet.track_event.track_uuid)
+        else:
+            resolved.append(defaults.get(sequence))
+    return resolved
+
+
+def check_validity(trace) -> list[dict]:
+    """Everything that can be wrong with a trace without knowing what it is *about*.
+
+    Each check is named in the problem it reports, so a caller asserts on the name rather than
+    on the wording of a message.
+    """
+    tracks = _effective_track_uuids(trace)
+    problems: list[dict] = []
+    problems += _check_sequence_ids(trace)
+    problems += _check_track_uuids_declared(trace, tracks)
+    problems += _check_slices_are_paired(trace, tracks)
+    return problems
+
+
+def _check_sequence_ids(trace) -> list[dict]:
+    """Every packet names the sequence it belongs to.
+
+    Stricter than the format demands — Perfetto tolerates packets outside any sequence — and
+    deliberately so. Interning and incremental state are sequence-scoped, so a packet that
+    escapes its sequence is far more likely a producer bug than a design. A producer that
+    genuinely needs one should be made to say so here.
+    """
+    return [
+        _problem("sequence_id", "packet carries no trusted_packet_sequence_id", index)
+        for index, packet in enumerate(trace.packet)
+        if not packet.HasField("trusted_packet_sequence_id")
+    ]
+
+
+def _check_track_uuids_declared(trace, tracks: list[int | None]) -> list[dict]:
+    """Every track a `TrackEvent` names was declared by some `TrackDescriptor`.
+
+    Declared *anywhere* in the trace, not necessarily earlier: descriptors and events may be
+    interleaved, and a reader that consumed the whole file resolves either order.
+    """
+    declared = {
+        packet.track_descriptor.uuid
+        for packet in trace.packet
+        if packet.WhichOneof("data") == "track_descriptor"
+    }
+    problems = []
+    for index, packet in enumerate(trace.packet):
+        if packet.WhichOneof("data") != "track_event":
+            continue
+        uuid = tracks[index]
+        if uuid is None:
+            problems.append(
+                _problem(
+                    "track_uuid",
+                    "track_event names no track, and its sequence declared no default",
+                    index,
+                )
+            )
+        elif uuid not in declared:
+            problems.append(
+                _problem("track_uuid", f"track {uuid} was never declared", index)
+            )
+    return problems
+
+
+def _check_slices_are_paired(trace, tracks: list[int | None]) -> list[dict]:
+    """Slices nest: on each track, every begin closes and no end arrives unopened."""
+    from perfetto.protos.perfetto.trace.perfetto_trace_pb2 import TrackEvent
+
+    open_slices: dict[int | None, list[int]] = {}
+    problems = []
+    for index, packet in enumerate(trace.packet):
+        if packet.WhichOneof("data") != "track_event":
+            continue
+        event = packet.track_event
+        track = tracks[index]
+        if event.type == TrackEvent.TYPE_SLICE_BEGIN:
+            open_slices.setdefault(track, []).append(index)
+        elif event.type == TrackEvent.TYPE_SLICE_END:
+            if not open_slices.get(track):
+                problems.append(
+                    _problem("slice_pairing", f"slice end on track {track} opened nothing", index)
+                )
+            else:
+                open_slices[track].pop()
+
+    # Sorted for a stable report, and keyed rather than compared directly: an event that names no
+    # track files its begins under `None`, and `None < 0` is a `TypeError`. Raised here it would
+    # take the whole dump down with exit 2 — the harness saying it could not run — and swallow the
+    # pairing problems it had already found. An unresolvable track sorts last.
+    for track, still_open in sorted(
+        open_slices.items(), key=lambda item: (item[0] is None, item[0] or 0)
+    ):
+        for index in still_open:
+            problems.append(
+                _problem("slice_pairing", f"slice begin on track {track} never ends", index)
+            )
+    return problems
+
+
+# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
+# The document
+# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
+
+
+def dump(path: Path, with_trace_processor: bool = True) -> dict:
+    """The whole document for one trace: what it says, and whether it holds together."""
+    from google.protobuf.json_format import MessageToDict
+    from google.protobuf.message import DecodeError
+    from perfetto.protos.perfetto.trace.perfetto_trace_pb2 import Trace
+
+    raw = path.read_bytes()
+    trace = Trace()
+    try:
+        trace.ParseFromString(raw)
+    except DecodeError as failure:
+        return {
+            "schema": SCHEMA,
+            "bytes": len(raw),
+            "validity": {
+                "ok": False,
+                "problems": [_problem("parses", f"not a Perfetto trace: {failure}")],
+            },
+            "wire": None,
+            "trace_processor": None,
+        }
+
+    problems = check_validity(trace)
+    return {
+        "schema": SCHEMA,
+        "bytes": len(raw),
+        "validity": {"ok": not problems, "problems": problems},
+        "wire": MessageToDict(trace, **RENDERING),
+        "trace_processor": trace_processor_view(path) if with_trace_processor else None,
+    }
+
+
+def render(document: dict) -> str:
+    """The document as bytes on stdout.
+
+    `sort_keys` so one trace always renders one way regardless of how a protobuf release
+    happens to order a message's fields; arrays keep the order they were built in, which is the
+    order the trace has.
+    """
+    return json.dumps(document, sort_keys=True, indent=2)
+
+
+def main(argv: list[str] | None = None) -> int:
+    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__.splitlines()[0])
+    parser.add_argument("trace", type=Path, help="path to a .perfetto-trace file")
+    parser.add_argument(
+        "--skip-trace-processor",
+        action="store_true",
+        help="wire view only; skips the query engine and the binary it downloads",
+    )
+    args = parser.parse_args(argv)
+
+    if not args.trace.is_file():
+        print(f"no trace at {args.trace}", file=sys.stderr)
+        return 2
+
+    # Anything that goes wrong *here* is the harness failing, not the trace being bad, and the
+    # two must not share an exit code — 1 tells a caller the file it handed over is malformed.
+    # The engine alone can fail half a dozen ways that are nothing to do with the trace: no
+    # network for its first download, a corrupt cached binary, a port it cannot bind, a load
+    # that times out. None of them is an `ImportError`, which is all this used to catch.
+    try:
+        document = dump(args.trace, with_trace_processor=not args.skip_trace_processor)
+    except ImportError as missing:
+        print(f"the harness needs the `perfetto` package: {missing}", file=sys.stderr)
+        return 2
+    except Exception:  # noqa: BLE001 - the harness failing is its own exit code
+        traceback.print_exc()
+        print("the harness could not read the trace; this is not a verdict on it", file=sys.stderr)
+        return 2
+
+    print(render(document))
+    return 0 if document["validity"]["ok"] else 1
+
+
+if __name__ == "__main__":
+    sys.exit(main())

+++ b/tests/harness/proto_constants.py
@@ -0,0 +1,183 @@
+"""Check a hand-maintained table of Perfetto field numbers against the official descriptors.
+
+An encoder that writes protobuf by hand owns a table of field numbers, and a wrong one fails
+**open**: the trace still parses, it just says something else. Nothing in the producer's own
+output can catch that, because its reader and its writer agree by construction. This re-derives
+each number from the schema that generated `perfetto_trace_pb2`.
+
+It knows nothing about who is asking. A claim is `(message, field, number)` or
+`(message, enum, value, number)`, and the answer is whether the schema agrees. What the caller
+intends to *write* into those fields is not visible here, and should not be.
+
+Usage:
+    python proto_constants.py CLAIMS      # a JSON file, or `-` for stdin
+
+The claims document:
+    {"fields": [["TracePacket", "timestamp", 8], ...],
+     "enums":  [["TrackEvent", "Type", "TYPE_SLICE_BEGIN", 1], ...]}
+
+A message is named by its path from the file: `ClockSnapshot.Clock` for a nested one. An enum
+declared at file scope rather than inside a message is claimed against the empty scope `""`.
+
+Exit codes: 0 every claim holds, 1 at least one does not, 2 the checker could not run (bad
+arguments, unreadable or malformed claims, missing dependency). The verdict is printed on
+stdout as JSON either way, so a caller reads *which* claim was wrong rather than inferring it.
+"""
+
+from __future__ import annotations
+
+import argparse
+import json
+import sys
+import traceback
+from pathlib import Path
+
+SCHEMA = "gcscope.proto-constants/1"
+
+
+def _problem(claim: str, detail: str) -> dict:
+    return {"claim": claim, "detail": detail}
+
+
+def _messages() -> dict:
+    """Every top-level message in the Perfetto trace schema, by name.
+
+    Nested messages are not in here and are not meant to be: they are reached through their
+    parent by [`_resolve_message`], so `Clock` on its own stays an unknown message rather than
+    resolving to whichever enclosing message happens to declare one.
+    """
+    from perfetto.protos.perfetto.trace import perfetto_trace_pb2
+
+    return dict(perfetto_trace_pb2.DESCRIPTOR.message_types_by_name)
+
+
+def _file_enums() -> dict:
+    """Every enum the file declares outside any message, by name — `BuiltinClock` among them.
+
+    Perfetto puts the clock domain ids at file scope, so a table naming one has no message to
+    hang it off. Claims spell that scope as the empty string.
+    """
+    from perfetto.protos.perfetto.trace import perfetto_trace_pb2
+
+    return dict(perfetto_trace_pb2.DESCRIPTOR.enum_types_by_name)
+
+
+def _resolve_message(name: str, messages: dict):
+    """A message by its path from the file: `TracePacket`, or `ClockSnapshot.Clock`.
+
+    `None` for anything the schema does not declare, including a path whose first step exists
+    and whose second does not — the caller reports that as an unknown message, which is what it
+    is. A dotted name is the only way to reach a nested message here, deliberately: resolving a
+    bare `Clock` by searching every parent would answer a question nobody asked.
+    """
+    head, _, rest = name.partition(".")
+    descriptor = messages.get(head)
+    while descriptor is not None and rest:
+        head, _, rest = rest.partition(".")
+        descriptor = descriptor.nested_types_by_name.get(head)
+    return descriptor
+
+
+def check_fields(claims: list, messages: dict) -> list[dict]:
+    """Each `(message, field, number)` against the schema's own number for that field."""
+    problems = []
+    for message, field, number in claims:
+        where = f"{message}.{field}"
+        descriptor = _resolve_message(message, messages)
+        if descriptor is None:
+            problems.append(_problem(where, f"no message named {message} in the schema"))
+            continue
+        actual = descriptor.fields_by_name.get(field)
+        if actual is None:
+            problems.append(_problem(where, f"{message} has no field named {field}"))
+        elif actual.number != number:
+            problems.append(
+                _problem(where, f"claimed field {number}, the schema says {actual.number}")
+            )
+    return problems
+
+
+def check_enums(claims: list, messages: dict, file_enums: dict) -> list[dict]:
+    """Each `(scope, enum, value, number)` against the schema's own value for that name.
+
+    `scope` is the message declaring the enum, or the empty string for one the file declares
+    outside any message. Both spellings report the same way, so a table does not have to know
+    which kind it is looking at until the schema disagrees with it.
+    """
+    problems = []
+    for message, enum, value, number in claims:
+        where = f"{message}.{enum}.{value}" if message else f"{enum}.{value}"
+        if message:
+            descriptor = _resolve_message(message, messages)
+            if descriptor is None:
+                problems.append(_problem(where, f"no message named {message} in the schema"))
+                continue
+            enum_descriptor = descriptor.enum_types_by_name.get(enum)
+        else:
+            enum_descriptor = file_enums.get(enum)
+        if enum_descriptor is None:
+            where_from = message or "the trace schema"
+            problems.append(_problem(where, f"{where_from} declares no enum named {enum}"))
+            continue
+        actual = enum_descriptor.values_by_name.get(value)
+        if actual is None:
+            problems.append(_problem(where, f"{enum} has no value named {value}"))
+        elif actual.number != number:
+            problems.append(
+                _problem(where, f"claimed value {number}, the schema says {actual.number}")
+            )
+    return problems
+
+
+def check(claims: dict) -> dict:
+    """The whole verdict for one claims document.
+
+    `checked` is reported rather than left implicit: a caller that handed over 55 claims and is
+    told 0 were checked has learnt something a bare "no problems" would have hidden.
+    """
+    messages = _messages()
+    fields = claims.get("fields", [])
+    enums = claims.get("enums", [])
+    problems = check_fields(fields, messages) + check_enums(enums, messages, _file_enums())
+    return {
+        "schema": SCHEMA,
+        "checked": {"fields": len(fields), "enums": len(enums)},
+        "ok": not problems,
+        "problems": problems,
+    }
+
+
+def render(verdict: dict) -> str:
+    return json.dumps(verdict, sort_keys=True, indent=2)
+
+
+def main(argv: list[str] | None = None) -> int:
+    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__.splitlines()[0])
+    parser.add_argument("claims", help="a JSON claims document, or `-` for stdin")
+    args = parser.parse_args(argv)
+
+    try:
+        text = sys.stdin.read() if args.claims == "-" else Path(args.claims).read_text()
+        claims = json.loads(text)
+    except (OSError, ValueError) as failure:
+        print(f"could not read the claims: {failure}", file=sys.stderr)
+        return 2
+
+    # A checker that cannot run must not answer "no problems". Anything that fails here is this
+    # file or its dependency, never the table it was given, so it takes an exit code of its own.
+    try:
+        verdict = check(claims)
+    except ImportError as missing:
+        print(f"the checker needs the `perfetto` package: {missing}", file=sys.stderr)
+        return 2
+    except Exception:  # noqa: BLE001 - the checker failing is its own exit code
+        traceback.print_exc()
+        print("the checker could not read the schema; this is not a verdict", file=sys.stderr)
+        return 2
+
+    print(render(verdict))
+    return 0 if verdict["ok"] else 1
+
+
+if __name__ == "__main__":
+    sys.exit(main())

diff --git a/tests/harness/reference_traces.py b/tests/harness/reference_traces.py
new file mode 100644
index 0000000..2acac2d
--- /dev/null
+++ b/tests/harness/reference_traces.py
@@ -0,0 +1,216 @@
+"""Perfetto traces authored with the protobuf bindings, for checking a decoder against.
+
+A decoder whose only input has ever been the encoder it is meant to check is a weak oracle: the
+two agree by construction and neither has been shown a third opinion. Everything here is built
+from `perfetto_trace_pb2` — at call time rather than committed as bytes, so the reference and
+the schema cannot drift apart on disk — and the harness has to report exactly what was put in.
+
+Nothing here is a GC trace. It is a process that runs a slice called `Work` with a `Detail`
+inside it and a counter that samples twice: enough shape to exercise nesting, annotations,
+counters and ordering rank, with no domain in it. A reader of this file should not be able to
+tell what gcscope writes.
+
+Usage:
+    python reference_traces.py KIND OUT    # KIND is one of the names in TRACES
+"""
+
+from __future__ import annotations
+
+import argparse
+import sys
+from pathlib import Path
+
+from perfetto.protos.perfetto.trace.perfetto_trace_pb2 import Trace, TrackEvent
+
+PROCESS_TRACK = 1
+THREAD_TRACK = 2
+COUNTER_TRACK = 3
+
+PROCESS_PID = 4242
+THREAD_TID = 7
+
+# The opening timestamp. Chosen with more significant digits than an IEEE double holds exactly,
+# so a renderer that turned 64-bit fields into JSON numbers would move it.
+FIRST_TS = 1_690_000_000_000_000_037
+LAST_TS = 1_690_000_000_000_000_900
+
+
+def _descriptor_packet(trace: Trace, uuid: int, name: str, sequence: int = 1):
+    packet = trace.packet.add()
+    packet.trusted_packet_sequence_id = sequence
+    packet.track_descriptor.uuid = uuid
+    packet.track_descriptor.name = name
+    return packet.track_descriptor
+
+
+def _event_packet(trace: Trace, uuid: int, ts: int, sequence: int = 1):
+    packet = trace.packet.add()
+    packet.trusted_packet_sequence_id = sequence
+    packet.timestamp = ts
+    packet.track_event.track_uuid = uuid
+    return packet.track_event
+
+
+def reference() -> Trace:
+    """One process, a thread track under it, a nested slice pair, and a counter."""
+    trace = Trace()
+
+    process = _descriptor_packet(trace, PROCESS_TRACK, f"Process {PROCESS_PID}")
+    process.process.pid = PROCESS_PID
+    # Written, and the harness must not confuse this with a field nobody touched.
+    process.sibling_order_rank = 0
+
+    thread = _descriptor_packet(trace, THREAD_TRACK, "Worker")
+    thread.parent_uuid = PROCESS_TRACK
+    thread.thread.pid = PROCESS_PID
+    thread.thread.tid = THREAD_TID
+
+    counter = _descriptor_packet(trace, COUNTER_TRACK, "queue_depth")
+    counter.parent_uuid = PROCESS_TRACK
+    counter.counter.unit_name = "items"
+
+    outer = _event_packet(trace, THREAD_TRACK, FIRST_TS)
+    outer.type = TrackEvent.TYPE_SLICE_BEGIN
+    outer.name = "Work"
+    outer.categories.append("demo")
+    annotation = outer.debug_annotations.add()
+    annotation.name = "attempt"
+    annotation.int_value = 3
+
+    inner = _event_packet(trace, THREAD_TRACK, 1_690_000_000_000_000_100)
+    inner.type = TrackEvent.TYPE_SLICE_BEGIN
+    inner.name = "Detail"
+    inner.categories.append("demo")
+
+    closing_inner = _event_packet(trace, THREAD_TRACK, 1_690_000_000_000_000_200)
+    closing_inner.type = TrackEvent.TYPE_SLICE_END
+    closing_inner.name = "Detail"
+
+    closing_outer = _event_packet(trace, THREAD_TRACK, LAST_TS)
+    closing_outer.type = TrackEvent.TYPE_SLICE_END
+    closing_outer.name = "Work"
+
+    for ts, value in ((1_690_000_000_000_000_100, 5), (LAST_TS, 2)):
+        sample = _event_packet(trace, COUNTER_TRACK, ts)
+        sample.type = TrackEvent.TYPE_COUNTER
+        sample.counter_value = value
+
+    return trace
+
+
+def track_from_defaults() -> Trace:
+    """A well-formed trace that names its track once, in the sequence's defaults.
+
+    Perfetto's standard way of not repeating a uuid on thousands of packets: state
+    `track_event_defaults.track_uuid` once and leave the field off every event. A checker that
+    reads only the explicit field calls this malformed — and files every event under track `0`,
+    where a begin on one track pairs with an end on another.
+    """
+    trace = Trace()
+    _descriptor_packet(trace, THREAD_TRACK, "Worker")
+
+    defaults = trace.packet.add()
+    defaults.trusted_packet_sequence_id = 1
+    defaults.trace_packet_defaults.track_event_defaults.track_uuid = THREAD_TRACK
+
+    for ts, kind, name in (
+        (FIRST_TS, TrackEvent.TYPE_SLICE_BEGIN, "Work"),
+        (LAST_TS, TrackEvent.TYPE_SLICE_END, "Work"),
+    ):
+        packet = trace.packet.add()
+        packet.trusted_packet_sequence_id = 1
+        packet.timestamp = ts
+        packet.track_event.type = kind  # no track_uuid: the sequence already said which
+        packet.track_event.name = name
+
+    return trace
+
+
+def undeclared_track() -> Trace:
+    """An event on a track no descriptor ever announced."""
+    trace = Trace()
+    _descriptor_packet(trace, PROCESS_TRACK, f"Process {PROCESS_PID}")
+    event = _event_packet(trace, 99, 1_000)
+    event.type = TrackEvent.TYPE_INSTANT
+    event.name = "orphan"
+    return trace
+
+
+def unmatched_begin() -> Trace:
+    """A slice that opens and never closes."""
+    trace = Trace()
+    _descriptor_packet(trace, THREAD_TRACK, "Worker")
+    begin = _event_packet(trace, THREAD_TRACK, 1_000)
+    begin.type = TrackEvent.TYPE_SLICE_BEGIN
+    begin.name = "never ends"
+    return trace
+
+
+def unopened_end() -> Trace:
+    """A slice that closes without having opened."""
+    trace = Trace()
+    _descriptor_packet(trace, THREAD_TRACK, "Worker")
+    end = _event_packet(trace, THREAD_TRACK, 1_000)
+    end.type = TrackEvent.TYPE_SLICE_END
+    end.name = "never began"
+    return trace
+
+
+def unclosed_on_a_named_and_an_unresolvable_track() -> Trace:
+    """Two slices left open: one on a declared track, one on no track at all.
+
+    The pair is the point. Events whose track cannot be resolved are filed under `None`, so a
+    trace holding both kinds makes the checker report a `None` key beside an integer one — and
+    ordering those against each other is where it used to raise instead of answering.
+    """
+    trace = Trace()
+    _descriptor_packet(trace, THREAD_TRACK, "Worker")
+
+    begin = _event_packet(trace, THREAD_TRACK, 1_000)
+    begin.type = TrackEvent.TYPE_SLICE_BEGIN
+    begin.name = "never ends"
+
+    packet = trace.packet.add()
+    packet.trusted_packet_sequence_id = 1
+    packet.timestamp = 2_000
+    packet.track_event.type = TrackEvent.TYPE_SLICE_BEGIN
+    packet.track_event.name = "never ends and names no track"
+    return trace
+
+
+def no_sequence_id() -> Trace:
+    """A packet belonging to no sequence."""
+    trace = Trace()
+    packet = trace.packet.add()
+    packet.track_descriptor.uuid = PROCESS_TRACK
+    packet.track_descriptor.name = f"Process {PROCESS_PID}"
+    return trace
+
+
+TRACES = {
+    "reference": reference,
+    "track-from-defaults": track_from_defaults,
+    "undeclared-track": undeclared_track,
+    "unmatched-begin": unmatched_begin,
+    "unopened-end": unopened_end,
+    "unclosed-mixed-tracks": unclosed_on_a_named_and_an_unresolvable_track,
+    "no-sequence-id": no_sequence_id,
+}
+
+
+def write(kind: str, path: Path) -> Path:
+    path.write_bytes(TRACES[kind]().SerializeToString())
+    return path
+
+
+def main(argv: list[str] | None = None) -> int:
+    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__.splitlines()[0])
+    parser.add_argument("kind", choices=sorted(TRACES))
+    parser.add_argument("out", type=Path)
+    args = parser.parse_args(argv)
+    write(args.kind, args.out)
+    return 0
+
+
+if __name__ == "__main__":
+    sys.exit(main())
diff --git a/tests/harness/requirements.txt b/tests/harness/requirements.txt
new file mode 100644
index 0000000..b218d0f
--- /dev/null
+++ b/tests/harness/requirements.txt
@@ -0,0 +1,23 @@
+# The verification harness's dependencies, declared here rather than installed by a bare
+# `pip install` in a workflow step, so a laptop and CI can reach the same state.
+#
+# Pinned exactly. The trace bytes gcscope writes do not depend on which interpreter a target
+# runs, so this leg gains nothing from a range and loses reproducibility: a decoder that
+# changes underneath a byte-for-byte assertion should be a commit someone made, not a Tuesday.
+#
+# This is NOT gcscope_probe's dependency list. That package is a distributable C extension
+# whose `requires-python = ">=3.13,<3.15"` is an ABI gate on internal struct layout; the
+# harness reads a file format and has no business inheriting an interpreter bound from it.
+# 0.57.2 rather than 0.56.0, and the two fields that force it are `TrackDescriptor`'s
+# `process_ordering` and `thread_ordering`. They are absent from 0.56.0's schema, so a
+# constant naming either one has nothing to be checked against, and gcscope writes both on the
+# root descriptor.
+#
+# This line used to add that 0.57 is where trace-processor starts exposing `y_axis_share_key` as
+# a column. It does not: 0.57.2's `counter_track` has no such column, which
+# `perfetto_dump.py`'s `counter_track_y_axis` query reports as data on every run. The field is
+# checked against the *schema* here — `proto_constants.py` finds it on `CounterDescriptor` — and
+# against the wire view in `tests/perfetto_encoder.rs`.
+perfetto==0.57.2
+protobuf==7.35.1
+pytest==8.3.5
diff --git a/tests/harness/test_perfetto_dump.py b/tests/harness/test_perfetto_dump.py
new file mode 100644
index 0000000..d9f6a64
--- /dev/null
+++ b/tests/harness/test_perfetto_dump.py
@@ -0,0 +1,368 @@
+"""Tests for the dump harness itself, against the traces in `reference_traces`.
+
+Those are authored with the protobuf bindings rather than by anything in this repo, which is
+the point: a decoder whose only input has ever been the encoder it is meant to check is a weak
+oracle, since the two agree by construction and neither has been shown a third opinion.
+
+The malformed cases matter as much as the well-formed one. A validity check nobody has watched
+reject something is a check that might only ever say yes.
+"""
+
+from __future__ import annotations
+
+import json
+import subprocess
+import sys
+from pathlib import Path
+
+import pytest
+
+sys.path.insert(0, str(Path(__file__).parent))
+
+import perfetto_dump  # noqa: E402
+import reference_traces  # noqa: E402
+from reference_traces import FIRST_TS, THREAD_TRACK, reference as reference_trace  # noqa: E402
+from perfetto.protos.perfetto.trace.perfetto_trace_pb2 import Trace  # noqa: E402
+
+HARNESS = Path(__file__).parent / "perfetto_dump.py"
+
+
+# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
+# Fixtures
+# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
+
+
+@pytest.fixture
+def write_trace(tmp_path):
+    def write(trace: Trace, name: str = "reference") -> Path:
+        path = tmp_path / f"{name}.perfetto-trace"
+        path.write_bytes(trace.SerializeToString())
+        return path
+
+    return write
+
+
+@pytest.fixture
+def reference(write_trace) -> Path:
+    return write_trace(reference_trace())
+
+
+def wire_dump(path: Path) -> dict:
+    """The wire half only. Nothing that asks about the format needs the query engine."""
+    return perfetto_dump.dump(path, with_trace_processor=False)
+
+
+# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
+# The wire view reports what was put in
+# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
+
+
+def test_every_packet_of_the_reference_trace_comes_back(reference):
+    document = wire_dump(reference)
+    packets = document["wire"]["packet"]
+
+    assert len(packets) == len(reference_trace().packet)
+    kinds = [next(k for k in p if k in ("track_descriptor", "track_event")) for p in packets]
+    assert kinds == ["track_descriptor"] * 3 + ["track_event"] * 6
+
+
+def test_a_slice_arrives_with_its_track_name_category_and_annotations(reference):
+    packets = wire_dump(reference)["wire"]["packet"]
+    opening = next(
+        p["track_event"]
+        for p in packets
+        if p.get("track_event", {}).get("name") == "Work"
+        and p["track_event"]["type"] == "TYPE_SLICE_BEGIN"
+    )
+
+    assert opening["track_uuid"] == str(THREAD_TRACK)
+    assert opening["categories"] == ["demo"]
+    assert opening["debug_annotations"] == [{"name": "attempt", "int_value": "3"}]
+
+
+def test_the_counter_samples_come_back_in_order(reference):
+    packets = wire_dump(reference)["wire"]["packet"]
+    samples = [
+        (p["timestamp"], p["track_event"]["counter_value"])
+        for p in packets
+        if p.get("track_event", {}).get("type") == "TYPE_COUNTER"
+    ]
+
+    assert samples == [
+        ("1690000000000000100", "5"),
+        ("1690000000000000900", "2"),
+    ]
+
+
+def test_a_field_nobody_expected_arrives_as_its_own_key(write_trace):
+    """The property that makes JSON worth the trouble.
+
+    Against a flat text dump, "the producer wrote something nobody asked for" is invisible to a
+    substring assertion — the unexpected token simply goes unread. Here the caller compares key
+    sets and the surprise fails a test.
+    """
+    trace = reference_trace()
+    trace.packet[0].track_descriptor.child_ordering = 2  # nobody asked for this
+    surprising = write_trace(trace, "surprising")
+
+    expected_keys = set(wire_dump(write_trace(reference_trace()))["wire"]["packet"][0]["track_descriptor"])
+    actual_keys = set(wire_dump(surprising)["wire"]["packet"][0]["track_descriptor"])
+
+    assert actual_keys - expected_keys == {"child_ordering"}
+
+
+# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
+# The three rendering decisions
+# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
+
+
+def test_field_names_are_the_ones_the_schema_uses(reference):
+    descriptor = wire_dump(reference)["wire"]["packet"][0]["track_descriptor"]
+
+    assert "sibling_order_rank" in descriptor
+    assert "siblingOrderRank" not in descriptor
+
+
+def test_a_written_zero_is_not_the_same_as_a_field_nobody_wrote(write_trace):
+    """The decision `always_print_fields_with_no_presence=False` turns on.
+
+    Perfetto's fields carry explicit presence, so an encoder that deliberately writes rank 0
+    says something a reader can see, and one that never touched the field says nothing. Print
+    the no-presence defaults instead and the two become the same document.
+    """
+    written = wire_dump(write_trace(reference_trace(), "written"))
+    first = written["wire"]["packet"][0]["track_descriptor"]
+    assert first["sibling_order_rank"] == 0
+
+    silent = reference_trace()
+    silent.packet[0].track_descriptor.ClearField("sibling_order_rank")
+    absent = wire_dump(write_trace(silent, "silent"))
+    assert "sibling_order_rank" not in absent["wire"]["packet"][0]["track_descriptor"]
+
+
+def test_64_bit_fields_are_strings_so_no_timestamp_is_rounded(reference):
+    """A nanosecond timestamp near 1.7e18 has more significant digits than a double holds.
+
+    The value below differs from its double-rounded self, so a renderer that emitted a JSON
+    number here would fail this test rather than quietly move an event.
+    """
+    packets = wire_dump(reference)["wire"]["packet"]
+    timestamps = [p["timestamp"] for p in packets if "timestamp" in p]
+
+    assert all(isinstance(t, str) for t in timestamps)
+    exact = FIRST_TS
+    assert str(exact) in timestamps
+    assert int(float(exact)) != exact, "the rounding this decision avoids"
+
+
+# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
+# Structural validity, and the traces it must reject
+# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
+
+
+def test_the_reference_trace_is_valid(reference):
+    validity = wire_dump(reference)["validity"]
+
+    assert validity["ok"] is True
+    assert validity["problems"] == []
+
+
+@pytest.mark.parametrize(
+    "kind,check",
+    [
+        ("undeclared-track", "track_uuid"),
+        ("unmatched-begin", "slice_pairing"),
+        ("unopened-end", "slice_pairing"),
+        ("no-sequence-id", "sequence_id"),
+    ],
+)
+def test_a_malformed_trace_is_rejected_by_the_check_that_owns_it(write_trace, kind, check):
+    validity = wire_dump(write_trace(reference_traces.TRACES[kind](), kind))["validity"]
+
+    assert validity["ok"] is False
+    assert [p["check"] for p in validity["problems"]] == [check]
+    assert validity["problems"][0]["packet"] is not None
+
+
+def test_a_track_named_once_in_the_sequence_defaults_is_still_named(write_trace):
+    """The standard producer pattern, which a naive checker rejects.
+
+    Two things go wrong at once when defaults are ignored: every event looks like it named no
+    track, and every event lands in bucket `0` — so a begin on one track would pair with an end
+    on another and the pairing check would go quiet exactly where it matters.
+    """
+    path = write_trace(reference_traces.track_from_defaults(), "defaults")
+    validity = wire_dump(path)["validity"]
+
+    assert validity["ok"] is True, validity["problems"]
+
+
+def test_an_event_on_a_sequence_with_no_default_and_no_track_is_still_caught(write_trace):
+    """Resolving defaults must not turn the check off for a trace that really is missing one.
+
+    `track_uuid` fires once per event and `slice_pairing` stays quiet, which is the intended
+    division: an event whose track cannot be resolved is already reported by the check that
+    owns that question, and the unresolvable ones share one bucket rather than being scattered
+    into track `0` where they would pair against real tracks.
+    """
+    trace = reference_traces.track_from_defaults()
+    del trace.packet[1]  # the defaults packet
+    validity = wire_dump(write_trace(trace, "no-defaults"))["validity"]
+
+    assert validity["ok"] is False

Bumps CodSpeedHQ/action from 5.0.1 to 5.6.0.

Release notes

Sourced from CodSpeedHQ/action's releases.

v5.6.0

Bumps the CodSpeed runner to v5.6.0.

Highlights

More consistent CPU Simulation results

Changes to your CI environment, like a different path or an extra environment variable, no longer change the performance. Each benchmark now starts with the same memory layout, reducing the chance of false regressions.

🐛 Bug Fixes

  • Keep the user's HOME when wrapping commands with sudo by @​lvaroqui in #588

⚙️ Internals

  • Bump pinned valgrind-codspeed to 3.26.0-0codspeed10 by @​adriencaccia in #593
    • fix(callgrind): suppress L3 warning for explicit LL settings by @​not-matthias in CodSpeedHQ/valgrind-codspeed#52
    • fix(initimg): stabilize Linux startup stack layout by @​not-matthias in CodSpeedHQ/valgrind-codspeed#53

Full Runner Changelog: https://github.com/CodSpeedHQ/codspeed/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md

What's Changed

  • chore: bump runner version to 5.6.0 by @​github-actions[bot] in CodSpeedHQ/action#253

Full Changelog: CodSpeedHQ/action@v5.5.0...v5.6.0

v5.5.0

Bumps the CodSpeed runner to v5.5.0.

This release adds support for Ubuntu 26.04, on both x86_64 and arm64. The officially supported distributions are now Ubuntu 22.04, 24.04 and 26.04, and Debian 12.

Profile uploads are also faster on GitHub-hosted runners, and archives larger than 5 GiB can now be uploaded.

Results from the Memory instrument are processed much faster and with less memory on large benchmarks.

This release also fixes a crash that could affect some pytest-codspeed benchmarks since v5.4.2.

🚀 Features

  • Split profile archive uploads into concurrent parts by @​lvaroqui in #565

🐛 Bug Fixes

  • Only set PYTHONPERFSUPPORT for exec-harness benchmarks by @​not-matthias in #584

⚡ Performance

  • Stream memtrack frames and decode them in parallel when finding module events by @​not-matthias in #578
